entries.fe72696e899789b25e4acea9adaa98a175ecb03c: <div sID="gen15455" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Isa.2" sID="Isa.2"/> <div eID="gen15455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15456" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15457" type="x-p"/> With this chapter begins a new sermon, which is continued in the two following chapters. The subject of this discourse is Judah and Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.1">ver. 1</reference>. In this chapter the prophet speaks, I. Of the glory of the Christians, Jerusalem, the gospel-church in the latter days, in the accession of many to it (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>), and the great peace it should introduce into the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">ver. 4</reference>), whence he infers the duty of the house of Jacob, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.5">ver. 5</reference>. II. Of the shame of the Jews, Jerusalem, as it then was, and as it would be after its rejection of the gospel and being rejected of God. 1. Their sin was their shame, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6-Isa.2.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. 2. God by his judgments would humble them and put them to shame, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.10-Isa.2.17">ver. 10-17</reference>. 3. They should themselves be ashamed of their confidence in their idols and in an arm of flesh, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.18-Isa.2.22">ver. 18-22</reference>. And now which of these Jerusalems will we be the inhabitants of—that which is full of the knowledge of God, which will be our everlasting honour, or that which is full of horses and chariots, and silver and gold, and such idols, which will in the end be our shame?
entries.c3d005aab039258486fbb6b3cdaac69322bb1415: <div eID="gen15457" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15456" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Increase of the Church Predicted. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15458" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> And it shall come to pass in the last days, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the mountain of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house shall be established in the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and all nations shall flow unto it. <hi type="super">3</hi> And many people shall go and say, Come ye, and let us go up to the mountain of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> from Jerusalem. <hi type="super">4</hi> And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning-hooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more. <hi type="super">5</hi> O house of Jacob, come ye, and let us walk in the light of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen15458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15459" type="x-p"/> The particular title of this sermon (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.1">v. 1</reference>) is the same with the general title of the book (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">ch. i. 1</reference>), only that what is there called the <hi type="italic">vision</hi> is here called <hi type="italic">the word which Isaiah saw</hi> (or the matter, or thing, which he saw), the truth of which he had as full an assurance of in his own mind as if he had seen it with his bodily eyes. Or this word was brought to him in a vision; something he saw when he received this message from God. John turned to <hi type="italic">see the voice</hi> that spoke with him. <reference osisRef="Rev.1.12">Rev. i. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen15459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15460" type="x-p"/> This sermon begins with the prophecy relating to the last days, the days of the Messiah, when his kingdom should be set up in the world, at the latter end of the Mosaic economy. In the last days of the earthly Jerusalem, just before the destruction of it, this heavenly Jerusalem should be erected, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">Heb. xii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Gal. iv. 26</reference>. Note, Gospel times are the last days. For 1. They were long in coming, were a great while waited for by the Old-Testament saints, and came at last. 2. We are not to look for any dispensation of divine grace but what we have in the gospel, <reference osisRef="Gal.1.8-Gal.1.9">Gal. i. 8, 9</reference>. 3. We are to look for the second coming of Jesus Christ at the end of time, as the Old-Testament saints did for his first coming; <hi type="italic">this is the last time,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.18">1 John ii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen15460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15461" type="x-p"/> Now the prophet here foretels, <div eID="gen15461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15462" type="x-p"/> I. The setting up of the Christian church, and the planting of the Christian religion, in the world. Christianity shall then be the mountain of the Lord's house; where that is professed God will grant his presence, receive his people's homage, and grant instruction and blessing, as he did of old in the temple of Mount Zion. The gospel church, incorporated by Christ's charter, shall then be the rendezvous of all the spiritual seed of Abraham. Now it is here promised, I. That Christianity shall be openly preached and professed; it shall be <hi type="italic">prepared</hi> (so the margin reads it) in the top of the mountains, in the view and hearing of all. Hence Christ's disciples are compared to a city on a hill, which <hi type="italic">cannot be hid,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.14">Matt. v. 14</reference>. They had many eyes upon them. Christ himself <hi type="italic">spoke openly to the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.20">John xviii. 20</reference>. What the apostles did was not <hi type="italic">done in a corner,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.26">Acts xxvi. 26</reference>. It was the lighting of a beacon, the setting up of a standard. Its being every where spoken <hi type="italic">against</hi> supposes that it was every where spoken <hi type="italic">of.</hi> 2. That is shall be firmly fixed and rooted; it shall be established on the top of the everlasting mountains, built upon a <hi type="italic">rock,</hi> so that the <hi type="italic">gates of hell shall not prevail against it,</hi> unless they could pluck up mountains by the roots. He that dwells safely is said to <hi type="italic">dwell on high,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">ch. xxxiii. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord has founded the gospel Zion.</hi> 3. That it shall not only overcome all opposition, but overtop all competition; it shall be <hi type="italic">exalted above the hills.</hi> This <hi type="italic">wisdom of God in a mystery</hi> shall outshine all the wisdom of this world, all its philosophy and all its politics. The spiritual worship which it shall introduce shall put down the idolatries of the heathen; and all other institutions in religion shall appear mean and despicable in comparison with this. See <reference osisRef="Ps.68.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>. <hi type="italic">Why leap ye, ye high hills? This is the hill which God desires to dwell in.</hi> <div eID="gen15462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15463" type="x-p"/> II. The bringing of the Gentiles into it. 1. The nations shall be admitted into it, even the uncircumcised, who were forbidden to come into the courts of the temple at Jerusalem. The partition wall, which kept them out, kept them off, shall be taken down. 2. <hi type="italic">All nations shall flow into it;</hi> having liberty of access, they shall improve their liberty, and multitudes shall embrace the Christian faith. They shall flow into it, as streams of water, which denotes the abundance of converts that the gospel should make and their speed and cheerfulness in coming into the church. They shall not be forced into it, but shall naturally flow into it. <hi type="italic">Thy people shall be willing,</hi> all volunteers, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. To Christ shall the <hi type="italic">gathering of the people be,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.10">Gen. xlix. 10</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Isa.60.4-Isa.60.5">ch. lx. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen15463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15464" type="x-p"/> III. The mutual assistance and encouragement which this confluence of converts shall give to one another. Their pious affections and resolutions shall be so intermixed that they shall come in in one full stream. As, when the Jews from all parts of the country went up thrice a year to worship at Jerusalem, they called on their friends in the road and excited them to go along with them, so shall many of the Gentiles court their relations, friends, and neighbours, to join with them in embracing the Christian religion (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord;</hi> though it be uphill and against the heart, yet it is <hi type="italic">the mountain of the Lord,</hi> who will assist the assent of our souls towards him." Note, Those that are entering into covenant and communion with God themselves should bring as many as they can along with them; it becomes Christians to provoke one another to good works, and to further the communion of saints by inviting one another into it: not, "Do you <hi type="italic">go up to the mountain of the Lord,</hi> and pray for us, and we will stay at home;" nor, "We will go, and do you do as you will;" but, "<hi type="italic">Come, and let us go,</hi> let us go in concert, that we may strengthen one another's hands and support one another's reputation:" not, "We will consider of it, and advise about it, and go hereafter;" but, <hi type="italic">Come, and let us go forthwith.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Ps.122.1">Ps. cxxii. 1</reference>. Many shall say this. Those that have had it said to them shall say it to others. The gospel church is here called, not only <hi type="italic">the mountain of the Lord,</hi> but <hi type="italic">the house of the God of Jacob;</hi> for in it God's covenant with Jacob and his praying seed is kept up and has its accomplishment; for to us now, as unto them, he never said, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.45.19">ch. xlv. 19</reference>. Now see here, 1. What they promise themselves in going up to the <hi type="italic">mountain of the Lord;</hi> There <hi type="italic">he will teach us of his ways.</hi> Note, God's ways are to be learned in his church, in communion with his people, and in the use of instituted ordinances—the ways of duty which he requires us to walk in, the ways of grace in which he walks towards us. It is God that teaches his people, by his word and Spirit. It is worth while to take pains to go up to his holy mountain to be taught his ways, and those who are willing to take that pains shall never find it labour in vain. Then <hi type="italic">shall we know if we follow on to know the Lord.</hi> 2. What they <hi type="italic">promise for themselves</hi> and one another: "If he will <hi type="italic">teach us his ways,</hi> we will <hi type="italic">walk in his paths;</hi> is he will let us know our duty, we will by his grace make conscience of doing it." Those who attend God's word with this humble resolution shall not be sent away without their lesson. <div eID="gen15464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15465" type="x-p"/> IV. The means by which this shall be brought about: <hi type="italic">Out of Zion shall go forth the law,</hi> the New-Testament law, the law of Christ, as of old the law of Moses from Mount Sinai, even <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.</hi> The gospel is a law, a law of faith; it is the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord;</hi> it <hi type="italic">went forth from Zion,</hi> where the temple was built, and from Jerusalem. Christ himself began in Galilee, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.23">Matt. iv. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.23.5">Luke xxiii. 5</reference>. But, when he commissioned his apostles to preach the gospel to all nations, he appointed them to begin in Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Luke xxiv. 47</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">Rom. xv. 19</reference>. Though most of them had their homes in Galilee, yet they must stay at Jerusalem, there to <hi type="italic">receive the promise of the Spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.4">Acts i. 4</reference>. And in the temple on Mount Zion they preached the gospel, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.20">Acts v. 20</reference>. This honour was allowed to Jerusalem, even after Christ was crucified there, for the sake of what it had been. And it was by this gospel, which took rise from Jerusalem, that the gospel church was <hi type="italic">established on the top of the mountains.</hi> This was the rod of divine strength, that was <hi type="italic">sent forth out of Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">Ps. cx. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen15465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15466" type="x-p"/> V. The erecting of the kingdom of the Redeemer in the world: <hi type="italic">He shall judge among the nations.</hi> He whose word goes forth out of Zion shall by that word not only subdue souls to himself, but rule in them, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">v. 4</reference>. He shall, in wisdom and justice, order and overrule the affairs of the world for the good of his church, and rebuke and restrain those that oppose his interest. By his Spirit working on men's consciences he shall judge, and rebuke shall try men and check them; his kingdom is spiritual, <hi type="italic">and not of this world.</hi> <div eID="gen15466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15467" type="x-p"/> VI. The great peace which should be the effect of the success of the gospel in the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall beat their swords into ploughshares;</hi> their instruments of war shall be converted into implements of husbandry; as, on the contrary, when war is proclaimed, <hi type="italic">ploughshares are beaten into swords,</hi> <reference osisRef="Joel.3.10">Joel iii. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Nations shall then not lift up sword against nation,</hi> as they now do, <hi type="italic">neither shall they learn war any more,</hi> for they shall have no more occasion for it. This does not make all war absolutely unlawful among Christians, nor is it a prophecy that in the days of the Messiah there shall be no wars. The Jews urge this against the Christians as an argument that Jesus is not the Messiah, because this promise is not fulfilled. But, 1. It was in part fulfilled in the peaceableness of the time in which Christ was born, when wars had in a great measure ceased, witness <hi type="italic">the taxing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.1">Luke ii. 1</reference>. 2. The design and tendency of the gospel are to make peace and to slay all enmities. It has in it the most powerful obligations and inducements to peace; so that one might reasonably have expected it should have this effect, and it would have had it if it had not been for those lusts of men from which come wars and fightings. 3. Jew and Gentiles were reconciled and brought together by the gospel, and there were no more such wars between them as there had been; for they became <hi type="italic">one sheepfold under one shepherd.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Eph.2.15">Eph. ii. 15</reference>. 4. The gospel of Christ, as far as it prevails, disposes men to be peaceable, softens men's spirits, and sweetens them; and the love of Christ, shed abroad in the heart, constrains men to love one another. 5. The primitive Christians were famous for brotherly love; their very adversaries took notice of it. 6. We have reason to hope that this promise shall yet have a more full accomplishment in the latter times of the Christian church, when the Spirit shall be poured out more plentifully from on high. Then there shall be on earth peace. <hi type="italic">Who shall live when God doeth this?</hi> But do it he will in due time, for <hi type="italic">he is not a man that he should lie.</hi> <div eID="gen15467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15468" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Here is a practical inference drawn from all this (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">O house of Jacob! come you, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.</hi> By the house of Jacob is meant either, 1. Israel according to the flesh. Let them be provoked by this <hi type="italic">to a holy emulation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">Rom. xi. 14</reference>. "Seeing the Gentiles are thus ready and resolved for God, thus forward to go up to the house of the Lord, let us stir up ourselves to go too. Let it never be said that the sinners of the Gentiles were better friends to the holy mountain than the house of Jacob." Thus the zeal of some should provoke many. Or, 2. Spiritual Israel, all that are brought to the God of Jacob. Shall there be such great knowledge in gospel times (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">v. 3</reference>) and such great peace (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">v. 4</reference>), and shall we share in these privileges? Come then, and let us live accordingly. What ever others do, <hi type="italic">come, O come!</hi> let us <hi type="italic">walk in the light of the Lord.</hi> (1.) Let us walk circumspectly in the light of this knowledge. Will God teach us his ways? Will he show us his glory in the face of Christ? Let us then <hi type="italic">walk as children of the light and of the day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Eph. v. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">1 Thess. v. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.12">Rom. xiii. 12</reference>. (2.) Let us walk comfortably in the light of this peace. Shall there be no more war? Let us then go on our way rejoicing, and let this joy terminate in God, and be our strength, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Neh. viii. 10</reference>. Thus shall we walk in the beams of the Sun of righteousness.
entries.43dc6ab46d02931b5862bc6c0ebfb032d472b56b: <div eID="gen15468" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Charge against the Israelites. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15469" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Therefore thou hast forsaken thy people the house of Jacob, because they be replenished from the east, and <hi type="italic">are</hi> soothsayers like the Philistines, and they please themselves in the children of strangers. <hi type="super">7</hi> Their land also is full of silver and gold, neither <hi type="italic">is there any</hi> end of their treasures; their land is also full of horses, neither <hi type="italic">is there any</hi> end of their chariots: <hi type="super">8</hi> Their land also is full of idols; they worship the work of their own hands, that which their own fingers have made: <hi type="super">9</hi> And the mean man boweth down, and the great man humbleth himself: therefore forgive them not. <div eID="gen15469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15470" type="x-p"/> The calling in of the Gentiles was accompanied with the rejection of the Jews; it was their fall, and the <hi type="italic">diminishing of them, that was the riches of the Gentiles;</hi> and the <hi type="italic">casting off of them</hi> was <hi type="italic">the reconciling of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.12-Rom.11.15">Rom. xi. 12-15</reference>); and it should seem that these verses have reference to that, and are designed to justify God therein, and yet it is probable that they are primarily intended for the convincing and awakening of the men of that generation in which the prophet lived, it being usual with the prophets to speak of the things that then were, both in mercy and judgment, as types of the things that should be hereafter. Here is, <div eID="gen15470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15471" type="x-p"/> I. Israel's doom. This is set forth in two words, the first and the last of this paragraph; but they are two dreadful words, and which speak, 1. Their case sad, very sad (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore thou hast forsaken thy people.</hi> Miserable is the condition of that people whom God has forsaken, and great certainly must the provocation be if he forsake those that have been his own people. This was the deplorable case of the Jewish church after they had rejected Christ. <hi type="italic">Migremus hinc—Let us go hence. Your house is left unto you desolate,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.38">Matt. xxiii. 38</reference>. Whenever any sore calamity came upon the Jews thus far the Lord might be said to forsake them that he withdrew his help and succour from them, else they would not have fallen into the hands of their enemies. But God never leaves any till they first leave him. 2. Their case desperate, wholly desperate (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore forgive them not.</hi> This prophetical prayer amounts to a threatening that they should not be forgiven, and some think it may be read: <hi type="italic">And thou wilt not forgive them.</hi> This refers not to particular persons (many of them repented and were pardoned), but to the body of that nation, against whom an irreversible doom was passed, that they should be wholly cut off and their church quite dismantled, never to be formed into such a body again, nor ever to have their old charter restored to them. <div eID="gen15471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15472" type="x-p"/> II. Israel's desert of this doom, and the reasons upon which it is grounded. In general, it is sin that brings destruction upon them; it is this, and nothing but this, that provokes God to forsake his people. The particular sins which the prophet specifies are such as abounded among them at that time, which he makes mention of for the conviction of those to whom he then preached, rather than that which afterwards proved the measure-filling sin, their crucifying Christ and persecuting his followers; for the sins of every age contributed towards the making up of the dreadful account at last. And there was a partial and temporary rejection of them by the captivity in Babylon hastening on, which was a type of their final destruction by the Romans, and which the sins here mentioned brought upon them. Their sins were such as directly contradicted all God's kind and gracious designs concerning them. <div eID="gen15472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15473" type="x-p"/> 1. God set them apart for himself, as a peculiar people, distinguished from, and dignified above, all other people (<reference osisRef="Num.23.9">Num. xxiii. 9</reference>); but they were <hi type="italic">replenished from the east;</hi> they <hi type="italic">naturalized</hi> foreigners, not <hi type="italic">proselyted,</hi> and encouraged them to settle among them, and mingled with them, <reference osisRef="Hos.7.8">Hos. vii. 8</reference>. Their country was peopled with Syrians and Chaldeans, Moabites and Ammonites, and other eastern nations, and with them they admitted the fashions and customs of those nations, and <hi type="italic">pleased themselves in the children of strangers,</hi> were fond of them, preferred their country before their own, and thought the more they conformed to them the more polite and refined they were; thus did they profane their crown and their covenant. Note, Those are in danger of being estranged from God who please themselves with those who are strangers to him, for we soon learn the ways of those whose company we love. <div eID="gen15473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15474" type="x-p"/> 2. God gave them his oracles, which they might ask counsel of, not only the scriptures and the seers, but the breast-plate of judgment; but they slighted these, and became soothsayers like the Philistines, introduced their arts of divination, and hearkened to those who by the stars, or the clouds, or the flight of birds, or the entrails of beasts, or other magic superstitions, pretended to discover things secret or foretel things to come. The Philistines were noted for diviners, <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.2">1 Sam. vi. 2</reference>. Note, Those who slight true divinity are justly given up to lying divinations; and those will certainly be forsaken of God who thus forsake him and their own mercies for lying vanities. <div eID="gen15474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15475" type="x-p"/> 3. God encouraged them to put their confidence in him, and assured them that he would be their wealth and strength; but, distrusting his power and promise, they made gold their hope, and furnished themselves with horses and chariots, and relied upon them for their safety, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.7">v. 7</reference>. God had expressly forbidden even their kings to multiply horses to themselves and <hi type="italic">greatly to multiply silver and gold,</hi> because he would have them to depend upon himself only; but they did not think their interest in God made them a match for their neighbours unless they had as full treasures of silver and gold, and as formidable hosts of chariots and horses, as they had. It is not having silver and gold, horses and chariots, that is a provocation to God, but, (1.) Desiring them insatiably, so that there is no end of the treasures, no end of the chariots, no bounds or limits set to the desire of them. Those shall never have enough in God (who alone is all-sufficient) that never know when they have enough of this world, which at the best is insufficient. (2.) Depending upon them, as if we could not be safe, and easy, and happy, without them, and could not but be so with them. <div eID="gen15475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15476" type="x-p"/> 4. God himself was their God, the sole object of their worship, and he himself instituted ordinances of worship for them; but they slighted both him and his institutions, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.8">v. 8</reference>. Their land was full of idols; every city had its god (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.13">Jer. xi. 13</reference>); and, according to the goodness of their lands, they made goodly images, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.1">Hos. x. 1</reference>. Those that think one God too little will find two too many, and yet hundreds were not sufficient; for those that love idols will multiply them; so sottish were they, and so wretchedly infatuated, that they <hi type="italic">worshipped the work of their own hands,</hi> as if that could be a god to them which was not only a creature, but <hi type="italic">their</hi> creature and that which their own fancies had devised and <hi type="italic">their own fingers had made.</hi> It was an aggravation of their idolatry that God had enriched them with silver and gold, and yet of that silver and gold they made idols; so it was, <hi type="italic">Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked,</hi> see <reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">Hos. ii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen15476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15477" type="x-p"/> 5. God had advanced them, and put honour upon them; but they basely diminished and disparaged themselves (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">The mean man boweth down to his idol,</hi> a thing below the meanest that has any spark of reason left. Sin is a disparagement to the poorest and those of the lowest rank. It becomes the mean man to bow down to his superiors, but it ill becomes him to <hi type="italic">bow down to the stock of a tree,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.19">ch. xliv. 19</reference>. Nor is it only the illiterate and poor-spirited that do this, but even the <hi type="italic">great men</hi> forgets his grandeur and humbles himself to worship idols, deifies men no better than himself, and consecrates stones so much baser than himself. Idolaters are said to <hi type="italic">debase themselves even to hell,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.57.9">ch. lvii. 9</reference>. What a shame it is that great men think the service of the true God below them and will not stoop to it, and yet will humble themselves to bow down to an idol! Some make this a threatening that the mean men shall be brought down, and the great men humbled, by the judgments of God, when they come with commission.
entries.5a81a01fe95344ac0590e9df13f95b1295aab2dd: <div eID="gen15477" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Doom of Idolaters. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 758.)</title> <div sID="gen15478" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Enter into the rock, and hide thee in the dust, for fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and for the glory of his majesty. <hi type="super">11</hi> The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> alone shall be exalted in that day. <hi type="super">12</hi> For the day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> upon every <hi type="italic">one that is</hi> proud and lofty, and upon every <hi type="italic">one that is</hi> lifted up; and he shall be brought low: <hi type="super">13</hi> And upon all the cedars of Lebanon, <hi type="italic">that are</hi> high and lifted up, and upon all the oaks of Bashan, <hi type="super">14</hi> And upon all the high mountains, and upon all the hills <hi type="italic">that are</hi> lifted up, <hi type="super">15</hi> And upon every high tower, and upon every fenced wall, <hi type="super">16</hi> And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all pleasant pictures. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> alone shall be exalted in that day. <hi type="super">18</hi> And the idols he shall utterly abolish. <hi type="super">19</hi> And they shall go into the holes of the rocks, and into the caves of the earth, for fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth. <hi type="super">20</hi> In that day a man shall cast his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which they made <hi type="italic">each one</hi> for himself to worship, to the moles and to the bats; <hi type="super">21</hi> To go into the clefts of the rocks, and into the tops of the ragged rocks, for fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and for the glory of his majesty, when he ariseth to shake terribly the earth. <hi type="super">22</hi> Cease ye from man, whose breath <hi type="italic">is</hi> in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of? <div eID="gen15478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15479" type="x-p"/> The prophet here goes on to show what a desolation would be brought upon their land when God should have forsaken them. This may refer particularly to their destruction by the Chaldeans first, and afterwards by the Romans, or it may have a general respect to the method God takes to awaken and humble proud sinners, and to put them out of conceit with that which they delighted in and depended on more than God. We are here told that sooner or later God will find out a way, <div eID="gen15479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15480" type="x-p"/> I. To startle and awaken secure sinners, who cry peace to themselves, and bid defiance to God and his judgments (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.10">v. 10</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Enter into the rock;</hi> God will attack you with such terrible judgments, and strike you with such terrible apprehensions of them, that you shall be forced to <hi type="italic">enter into the rock, and hide yourself in the dust, for fear of the Lord.</hi> You shall lose all your courage, and tremble at the shaking of a leaf; your heart shall <hi type="italic">fail you for fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.26">Luke xxi. 26</reference>), and you shall <hi type="italic">flee when none pursues,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Prov. xxviii. 1</reference>. To the same purport, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.19">v. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">They shall go into the holes of the rocks, and into the caves of the earth,</hi> the darkest the deepest places; they shall <hi type="italic">call to the rocks and mountains to fall on them,</hi> and rather crush them than not cover them, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.8">Hos. x. 8</reference>. It was so particularly at the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.30">Luke xxiii. 30</reference>) and of the persecuting pagan powers, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Rev. vi. 16</reference>. And all <hi type="italic">for fear of the Lord, and of the glory of his majesty,</hi> looking upon him then to be a consuming fire and themselves as stubble before him, <hi type="italic">when he arises to shake terribly the earth,</hi> to <hi type="italic">shake the wicked out of it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.13">Job xxxviii. 13</reference>), and to shake all those earthly props and supports with which they have buoyed themselves up, to shake them from under them. Note, 1. <hi type="italic">With God is terrible majesty,</hi> and the glory of it is such as sooner or later will oblige us all to flee before him. 2. Those that will not fear God and flee to him will be forced to fear him and flee from him to a refuge of lies. 3. It is folly for those that are pursued by the wrath of God to think to escape it, and to hide or shelter themselves from it. 4. The things of the earth are things that will be shaken; they are subject to concussions, and hastening towards a dissolution. 5. The shaking of the earth is, and will be, a terrible thing to those who set their affections wholly on things of the earth. 6. It will be in vain to think of finding refuge in the caves of the earth when the earth itself is shaken; there will be no shelter then but in God and in things above. <div eID="gen15480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15481" type="x-p"/> II. To humble and abase proud sinners, that look big, and think highly of themselves, and scornfully of all about them (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The lofty looks of man shall be humbled.</hi> The eyes that aim high, the countenance in which the pride of the heart shows itself, shall be cast down in shame and despair. And the <hi type="italic">haughtiness of men shall be bowed down,</hi> their spirits shall be broken, and they shall be crest-fallen, and those things which they were proud of they shall be ashamed of. It is repeated (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">The loftiness of man shall be bowed down.</hi> Note, Pride will, one way or other, have a fall. Men's haughtiness will be brought down, either by the grace of God convincing them of the evil of their pride, and clothing them with humility, or by the providence of God depriving them of all those things they were proud of and laying them low. Our Saviour often laid it down for a maxim that <hi type="italic">he who exalts himself shall be abased;</hi> he shall either abase himself in true repentance or God will abase him and pour contempt upon him. Now here we are told, <div eID="gen15481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15482" type="x-p"/> 1. Why this shall be done: because the <hi type="italic">Lord alone will be exalted.</hi> Note, Proud men shall be vilified because the Lord alone will be magnified. It is for the honour of God's power to humble the proud; by this he proves himself to be God, and disproves Job's pretensions to rival with him, <reference osisRef="Job.40.11-Job.40.14">Job xl. 11-14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Behold every one that is proud, and abase him; then will I also confess unto thee.</hi> It is likewise for the honour of his justice. Proud men stand in competition with God, who is jealous for his own glory, and will not suffer men either to take to themselves or give to another that which is due to him only. They likewise stand in opposition to God; they resist him, and therefore he resists them; for he <hi type="italic">will be exalted among the heathen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.46.10">Ps. xlvi. 10</reference>), and there is a day coming in which he alone will be exalted, when he shall have put <hi type="italic">down all opposing rule, principality, and power,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1 Cor. xv. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen15482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15483" type="x-p"/> 2. How this shall be done: by humbling judgments, that shall mortify men, and bring them down (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">The day of the Lord of hosts,</hi> the day of his wrath and judgment, <hi type="italic">shall be upon every one that is proud.</hi> He now laughs at their insolence because he sees that his day is coming, this day, which will be upon them ere they are aware, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.13">Ps. xxxvii. 13</reference>. This day of the Lord is here said to be upon <hi type="italic">all the cedars of Lebanon, that are high and lifted up.</hi> Jerome observes that the cedars are said to praise God (<reference osisRef="Ps.148.9">Ps. cxlviii. 9</reference>) and are <hi type="italic">trees of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.16">Ps. civ. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">of his planting</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.19">Isa. xli. 19</reference>), and yet here God's wrath fastens upon the cedars, which denotes (says he) that some of every rank of men, some great men, will be saved, and some perish. It is brought in as an instance of the strength of God's voice that it <hi type="italic">breaks the cedars</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.5">Ps. xxix. 5</reference>), and here the day of the Lord is said to be <hi type="italic">upon the cedars,</hi> those of Lebanon, they were the straightest and statliest,—upon the oaks, those of Bashan, that were the strongest and sturdiest,—upon the natural elevations and fortresses, <hi type="italic">the highest mountains and the hills that are lifted up</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.14">v. 14</reference>), that overtop the valleys and seem to push the skies,—and upon the artificial fastnesses, <hi type="italic">every high tower and every fenced wall,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.15">v. 15</reference>. Understand these, (1.) As representing the proud people themselves, that are in their own apprehensions like the cedars and the oaks, firmly rooted, and not to be stirred by any storm, and looking on all around them as shrubs; these are the high mountains and the lofty hills that seem to fill the earth, that are gazed on by all, and think themselves immovable, but lie most obnoxious to God's thunderstrokes. <hi type="italic">Feriuntique summos fulmina montes—The highest hills are most exposed to lightning.</hi> And before the power of God's wrath these mountains are scattered and these hills bow and <hi type="italic">melt like wax,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Hab. iii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.8">Ps. lxvi. 8</reference>. These vaunting men, who are as high towers in which the noisy bells are hung, on which the thundering murdering cannon are planted—these fenced walls, that fortify themselves with their native hardiness, and intrench themselves in their fastnesses—shall be brought down. (2.) As particularizing the things they are proud of, in which they trust, and of which they make their boast. The day of the Lord shall be upon those very things in which they put their confidence as their strength and security; he will <hi type="italic">take from them all their armour wherein they trusted.</hi> Did the inhabitants of Lebanon glory in their cedars, and those of Bashan in their oaks, such as no country could equal? The day of the Lord should rend those cedars, those oaks, and the houses built of them. Did Jerusalem glory in the mountains that were round about it, as its impregnable fortifications, or in its walls and bulwarks? These should be levelled and laid low in the day of the Lord. Besides those things that were for their strength and safety they were proud, [1.] Of their trade abroad; but the day of the Lord shall be <hi type="italic">upon all the ships of Tarshish;</hi> they shall be broken as Jehoshaphat's were, shall founder at sea or be ship-wrecked in harbour. Zebulun was a haven of ships, but should now no more rejoice in his going out. When God is bringing ruin upon a people he can sink all the branches of their revenue. [2.] Of their ornaments at home; but the day of the Lord shall be <hi type="italic">upon all pleasant pictures,</hi> the painting of their ships (so some understand it) or the curious pieces of painting they brought home in their ships from other countries, perhaps from Greece, which afterwards was famous for painters. Upon <hi type="italic">every thing that is beautiful to behold;</hi> so some read it. Perhaps they were the pictures of their relations, and for that reason pleasant, or of their gods, which to the idolaters were delectable things; or they admired them for the fineness of their colours or strokes. There is no harm in making pictures, nor in adorning our rooms with them, provided they transgress not either the second or the seventh commandment. But to place our pictures among our pleasant things, to be fond of them and proud of them, to spend that upon them which should be laid out in charity, and to set our hearts upon them, as it ill becomes those who have so many substantial things to take pleasure in, so it tends to provoke God to strip us of all such vain ornaments. <div eID="gen15483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15484" type="x-p"/> III. To make idolaters ashamed of their idols, and of all the affection they have had for them and the respect they have paid to them (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The idols he shall utterly abolish.</hi> When the Lord alone shall be exalted (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.17">v. 17</reference>) he will not only pour contempt upon proud men, who like Pharaoh exalt themselves against him, but much more upon all pretended deities, who are rivals with him for divine honours. They shall be abolished, utterly abolished. Their friends shall desert them; their enemies shall destroy them; so that, one way or other, an utter riddance shall be made of them. See here, 1. The vanity of false gods; they cannot secure themselves, so far are they from being able to secure their worshippers. 2. The victory of the true God over them; for <hi type="italic">great is the truth and will prevail.</hi> Dagon fell before the ark, and Baal before the Lord God of Elijah. The gods of the heathen shall be famished (<reference osisRef="Zeph.2.11">Zeph. ii. 11</reference>), and by degrees shall perish, <reference osisRef="Jer.10.11">Jer. x. 11</reference>. The rightful Sovereign will triumph over all pretenders. And, as God will abolish idols, so their worshippers shall abandon them, either from a gracious conviction of their vanity and falsehood (as Ephraim when he said, <hi type="italic">What have I to do any more with idols?</hi>) or from a late and sad experience of their inability to help them, and a woeful despair of relief by them, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">v. 20</reference>. When men are themselves frightened by the judgments of God into the holes of the rocks and caves of the earth, and find that they do thus in vain shift for their own safety, they shall cast their idols, which they have made their gods, and hoped to make their friends in the time of need, to the moles and to the bats, any where out of sight, that, being freed from the incumbrance of them, they may <hi type="italic">go into the clefts of the rocks, for fear of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.21">v. 21</reference>. Note, (1.) Those that will not be reasoned out of their sins sooner or later shall be frightened out of them. (2.) God can make men sick of those idols that they have been most fond of, even the idols of silver and the idols of gold, the most precious. Covetous men make silver and gold their idols, money their god; but the time may come when they may feel it as much their burden as ever they made it their confidence, and may find themselves as much exposed by it as ever they hoped they should be guarded by it, when it tempts their enemy, sinks their ship, or retards their flight. There was a time when the mariners threw the wares, and even the <hi type="italic">wheat into the sea</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.5">Jonah i. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.27.38">Acts xxvii. 38</reference>), and the <hi type="italic">Syrians cast away their garments for haste,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.7.15">2 Kings vii. 15</reference>. Or men may cast it away out of indignation at themselves for leaning upon such a broken reed. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.19">Ezek. vii. 19</reference>. The idolaters here throw away their idols because they are ashamed of them and of their own folly in trusting to them, or because they are afraid of having them found in their possession when the judgments of God are abroad; as the thief throws away his stolen goods then he is searched for or pursued. (3.) The darkest holes, where the moles and the bats lodge, are the fittest places for idols, that have eyes and see not; and God can force men to cast their own idols there (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">ch. xxx. 22</reference>), when they are <hi type="italic">ashamed of the oaks which they have desired,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">ch. i. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">Moab shall be ashamed of Chemosh, as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.13">Jer. xlviii. 13</reference>. (4.) It is possible that sin may be both loathed and left and yet not truly repented of—loathed because surfeited on, left because there is no opportunity of committing it, yet not repented of out of any love to God, but only from a slavish fear of his wrath. <div eID="gen15484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15485" type="x-p"/> IV. To make those that have trusted in an arm of flesh ashamed of their confidence (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.22">v. 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Cease from man.</hi> The providences of God concerning you shall speak this aloud to you, and therefore take warning beforehand, that you may prevent the uneasiness and shame of disappointment; and consider, 1. How weak man is: <hi type="italic">His breath is in his nostrils,</hi> puffed out every moment, soon gone for good and all." Man is a dying creature, and may die quickly; our nostrils, in which our breath is, are of the outward parts of the body; what is there is like one standing at the door, ready to depart; nay the doors of the nostrils are always open, the breath in them may slip away ere we are aware, in a moment. Wherein then is man to be accounted of? Alas! no reckoning is to be made of him, for he is not what he seems to be, what he pretends to be, what we fancy him to be. Man is like vanity, nay, he is vanity, he is altogether vanity, he is less, he is lighter, than vanity, when weighed in the balance of the sanctuary. "2. How wise therefore those are that cease from man;" it is our duty, it is our interest, to do so. "<hi type="italic">Put not your trust in man,</hi> nor make even the greatest and mightiest of men your confidence; cease to do so. Let not your eye be to the power of man, for it is finite and limited, derived and depending; it is not from him that your judgment proceeds. Let not him be your fear, let not him be your hope; but look up to the power of God, to which all the powers of men are subject and subordinate; dread his wrath, secure his favour, take him for your help, and let your <hi type="italic">hope be in the Lord your God.</hi>"  <chapter eID="Isa.2"/> <div eID="gen15485" type="x-p"/>

entries.644ea824f264a4f9abdd719f69e53992ca9edc22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8338"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen13296" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.1-Isa.2.22">Is 2:1-22</reference>.<div eID="gen13296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8338"/>1. The inscription.<div eID="gen13297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The word--</hi>the revelation. <div eID="gen13298" type="x-p"/>
entries.3de2d6ed50d73ea7f5161618b41d567e95c32568: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8339"/><div sID="gen13299" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8339"/>2. Same as <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1">Mi 4:1</reference>. As Micah prophesied in Jotham's reign, and Isaiah in Uzziah's, Micah rests on Isaiah, whom he confirms: not vice versa. Hengstenberg on slight grounds makes <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1">Mi 4:1</reference> the original.<div eID="gen13299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">last days--</hi>that is, Messiah's: especially the days yet to come, to which all prophecy hastens, when "the house of the God of Jacob," namely, at Jerusalem, shall be the center to which the converted nations shall flock together (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.32">Mt 13:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.31">Lu 2:31</reference>, 32; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.6">Ac 1:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>); where "the kingdom" of Israel is regarded as certain and the time alone uncertain (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.15">Psa 68:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.8">72:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen13300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13301" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mountain of the Lord's house ... in the top, &c.--</hi>the temple on Mount Moriah: type of the Gospel, beginning at Jerusalem, and, like an object set on the highest hill, made so conspicuous that all nations are attracted to it.<div eID="gen13301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flow--</hi>as a broad stream (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.12">Is 66:12</reference>). <div eID="gen13302" type="x-p"/>
entries.2922c02c2ee538c7ebd33f60a342b2576efd109a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8340"/><div sID="gen13303" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8340"/>3. If the curse foretold against Israel has been literally fulfilled, so shall the promised blessing be literal. We Gentiles must not, while giving them the curse, deny them their peculiar blessing by spiritualizing it. The Holy Ghost shall be poured out for a general conversion then (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">Jr 50:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.8.21">Zec 8:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joe 2:28</reference>).<div eID="gen13303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Jerusalem--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Luke.24.47">Lu 24:47</reference>) an earnest of the future relations of Jerusalem to Christendom (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.12">Ro 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.15">15</reference>). <div eID="gen13304" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa98a38836024505305eaf00b0fa400d0d30fe64: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8341"/><div sID="gen13305" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8341"/><hi type="bold">4. judge--</hi>as a sovereign umpire, settling all controversies (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.4">Is 11:4</reference>). Lowth translates "work," "conviction."<div eID="gen13305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plowshares--</hi>in the East resembling a short sword (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.10">Zec 9:10</reference>). <div eID="gen13306" type="x-p"/>
entries.246d38ebc54d49bffb3c711d0d3040ee340e6df0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8342"/><div sID="gen13307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8342"/>5. The connection is: As Israel's high destiny is to be a blessing to all nations (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Ge 12:3</reference>), let Israel's children walk worthy of it (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Ep 5:8</reference>). <div eID="gen13307" type="x-p"/>
entries.6ef8a6536fc81924368c852ba921feb9ae958354: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8343"/><div sID="gen13308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8343"/><hi type="bold">6. Therefore--</hi>rather, "For": reasons why there is the more need of the exhortation in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.5">Is 2:5</reference>.<div eID="gen13308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou--</hi>transition to Jehovah: such rapid transitions are natural, when the mind is full of a subject.<div eID="gen13309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">replenished--</hi>rather, filled, namely, with the superstitions of the East, Syria, and Chaldea.<div eID="gen13310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">soothsayers--</hi>forbidden (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.10-Deut.18.14">De 18:10-14</reference>).<div eID="gen13311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13312" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Philistines--</hi>southwest of Palestine: antithesis to "the east."<div eID="gen13312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">please themselves--</hi>rather, join hands with, that is, enter into alliances, matrimonial and national: forbidden (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.32">Ex 23:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.13.23">Ne 13:23</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen13313" type="x-p"/>
entries.ba3dcb8d8dba7085b3f019c67c6ab8212458f819: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8344"/><div sID="gen13314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8344"/><hi type="bold">7. gold--</hi>forbidden to be heaped together (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.17">De 17:17</reference>). Solomon disobeyed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.21">1Ki 10:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.27">27</reference>).<div eID="gen13314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horses ... chariots--</hi>forbidden (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">De 17:16</reference>). But Solomon disobeyed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.26">1Ki 20:26</reference>). Horses could be used effectively for war in the plains of Egypt; not so in the hilly Judea. God designed there should be as wide as possible a distinction between Israel and the Egyptians. He would have His people wholly dependent on Him, rather than on the ordinary means of warfare (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>). Also horses were connected with idolatry (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">2Ki 23:11</reference>); hence His objection: so the transition to "idols" (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.8">Is 2:8</reference>) is natural. <div eID="gen13315" type="x-p"/>
entries.b53ef492cd678a86dc37548d2da6cf2a578712e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8345"/><div sID="gen13316" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8345"/>8. (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.4">Ho 8:4</reference>). Not so much public idolatry, which was not sanctioned in Uzziah's and Jotham's reign, but (see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.4">2Ki 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.35">35</reference>) as private. <div eID="gen13316" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f93080cfe424136e45a7157b3dc78a5a9204b3e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8346"/><div sID="gen13317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8346"/><hi type="bold">9. mean--</hi>in rank: not morally base: opposed to "the great man." The former is in Hebrew, Adam, the latter, ish.<div eID="gen13317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">boweth--</hi>namely, to idols. All ranks were idolaters.<div eID="gen13318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forgive ... not--</hi>a threat expressed by an imperative. Isaiah so identifies himself with God's will, that he prays for that which he knows God purposes. So <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">Re 18:6</reference>. <div eID="gen13319" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e7cd39e981810699890678ca6a560c472ddff19: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8347"/><div sID="gen13320" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8347"/>10. Poetical form of expressing that, such were their sins, they would be obliged by God's judgments to seek a hiding-place from His wrath (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Re 6:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen13320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dust--</hi>equivalent to "caves of the earth," or dust (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.19">Is 2:19</reference>).<div eID="gen13321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for fear, &c.--</hi>literally, "from the face of the terror of the Lord." <div eID="gen13322" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8f855d7e1d76f2dcc81de24c697c794b094695d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8348"/><div sID="gen13323" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8348"/><hi type="bold">11. lofty looks--</hi>literally, "eyes of pride" (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.27">Psa 18:27</reference>).<div eID="gen13323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">humbled--</hi>by calamities. God will so vindicate His honor "in that day" of judgments, that none else "shall be exalted" (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.9">Zec 14:9</reference>). <div eID="gen13324" type="x-p"/>
entries.da523e7f70cf9d2882fffc079b6fd9a75a5eee8f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8349"/><div sID="gen13325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8349"/>12. Man has had many days: "the day of the Lord" shall come at last, beginning with judgment, a never-ending day in which God shall be "all in all" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.28">1Co 15:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">2Pe 3:10</reference>).<div eID="gen13325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every--</hi>not merely person, as English Version explains it, but every thing on which the nation prided itself. <div eID="gen13326" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f25df36ab835f13d30c8d4ddc74de82f6b7e129: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8350"/><div sID="gen13327" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8350"/><hi type="bold">13. cedars ... oaks--</hi>image for haughty nobles and princes (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.9">Am 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.11.1">Zec 11:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.19.18-Rev.19.21">Re 19:18-21</reference>).<div eID="gen13327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bashan--</hi>east of Jordan, north of the river Jabbok, famous for fine oaks, pasture, and cattle. Perhaps in "oaks" there is reference to their idolatry (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Is 1:29</reference>). <div eID="gen13328" type="x-p"/>
entries.e07ebb6ee8d78ef88f484ff74643fc6cabf32eaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8351"/><div sID="gen13329" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8351"/><hi type="bold">14. high ... hills--</hi>referring to the "high places" on which sacrifices were unlawfully offered, even in Uzziah's (equivalent to Azariah) reign (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.4">2Ki 15:4</reference>). Also, places of strength, fastnesses in which they trusted, rather than in God; so <div eID="gen13329" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfb93a0dd4b5ad323fd9ebbfa9e42a2b8d61b1db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8352"/><div sID="gen13330" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8352"/><hi type="bold">15. tower ... wall--</hi>Towers were often made on the walls of cities.<div eID="gen13330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fenced--</hi>strongly fortified. <div eID="gen13331" type="x-p"/>
entries.56377aaa3b9da4328ecc2069ad912cc3083b2ade: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8353"/><div sID="gen13332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8353"/><hi type="bold">16. Tarshish--</hi>Tartessus in southwest Spain, at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, near Gibraltar. It includes the adjoining region: a Phoenician colony; hence its connection with Palestine and the Bible (<reference osisRef="2Chr.9.21">2Ch 9:21</reference>). The name was also used in a wide sense for the farthest west, as our West Indies (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.19">Is 66:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.7">Psa 48:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.72.10">72:10</reference>). "Ships of Tarshish" became a phrase for richly laden and far-voyaging vessels. The judgment shall be on all that minister to man's luxury (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.18.17-Rev.18.19">Re 18:17-19</reference>).<div eID="gen13332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pictures--</hi>ordered to be destroyed (<reference osisRef="Num.33.52">Nu 33:52</reference>). Still to be seen on the walls of Nineveh's palaces. It is remarkable that whereas all other ancient civilized nations, Egypt, Assyria, Greece, Rome, have left monuments in the fine arts, Judea, while rising immeasurably above them in the possession of "the living oracles," has left none of the former. The fine arts, as in modern Rome, were so often associated with polytheism, that God required His people in this, as in other respects, to be separate from the nations (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.15-Deut.4.18">De 4:15-18</reference>). But Vulgate translation is perhaps better, "All that is beautiful to the sight"; not only paintings, but all luxurious ornaments. One comprehensive word for all that goes before (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.18.12">Re 18:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.16">14, 16</reference>). <div eID="gen13333" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e0f51cf3ae9189290ea461e82edf6b02cbc1bf5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8354"/><div sID="gen13334" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8354"/>17. Repeated from <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Is 2:11</reference>, for emphatic confirmation. <div eID="gen13334" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3ff1ac7689c25e53752b17b90dafba213ccbbcd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8355"/><div sID="gen13335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8355"/><hi type="bold">18. idols--</hi>literally, "vain things," "nothings" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.8.4">1Co 8:4</reference>). Fulfilled to the letter. Before the Babylonian captivity the Jews were most prone to idolatry; in no instance, ever since. For the future fulfilment, see <reference osisRef="Zech.13.2">Zec 13:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.15">Re 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.20">19:20</reference>. <div eID="gen13335" type="x-p"/>
entries.516c8ad87466070268295a07b0005ae51cb4bd45: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8356"/><div sID="gen13336" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8356"/>19. The fulfilment answers exactly to the threat (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.10">Is 2:10</reference>).<div eID="gen13336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they--</hi>the idol-worshippers.<div eID="gen13337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">caves--</hi>abounding in Judea, a hilly country; hiding-places in times of alarm (<reference osisRef="1Sam.13.6">1Sa 13:6</reference>).<div eID="gen13338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shake ... earth--</hi>and the heavens also (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.26">He 12:26</reference>). Figure for severe and universal judgments. <div eID="gen13339" type="x-p"/>
entries.99296adfced924dd403f460898891e92feaa9bb0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8357"/><div sID="gen13340" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8357"/><hi type="bold">20. moles--</hi>Others translate "mice." The sense is, under ground, in darkness.<div eID="gen13340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13341" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bats--</hi>unclean birds (<reference osisRef="Lev.11.19">Le 11:19</reference>), living amidst tenantless ruins (<reference osisRef="Rev.11.13">Re 11:13</reference>). <div eID="gen13341" type="x-p"/>
entries.d2953c38baebe86962afb02cab014424513ae93c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8358"/><div sID="gen13342" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8358"/>22. The high ones (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Is 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.13">13</reference>) on whom the people trust, shall be "brought low" (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.2">Is 3:2</reference>); therefore "cease from" depending on them, instead of on the Lord (<reference osisRef="Ps.146.3-Ps.146.5">Psa 146:3-5</reference>). <chapter eID="Isa.2"/>

entries.1042e2d360167a7942fd92c9f9817b42115588cd: <div eID="gen26468" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26469" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26470" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26470" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26469" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26471" type="x-p"/> Prophecy concerning the kingdom of the Messiah, and the conversion of the Gentile world, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.1-Isa.2.5">Isa 2:1-5</reference>. Great wickedness and idolatry of the unbelieving Jews, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6-Isa.2.9">Isa 2:6-9</reference>. Terrible consternation that will seize the wicked, who shall in vain seek for rocks and mountains to hide them from the face of God in the day of his judgments, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.10-Isa.2.17">Isa 2:10-17</reference>. Total destruction of idolatry in consequence of the establishment of Messiah's kingdom, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.18-Isa.2.21">Isa 2:18-21</reference>. An exhortation to put no confidence in man, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.22">Isa 2:22</reference>. <div eID="gen26471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26472" type="x-p"/> The prophecy contained in the second, third, and fourth chapters, makes one continued discourse. The first five verses of chap. 2 foretell the kingdom of Messiah, the conversion of the Gentiles, and their admission into it. From the sixth verse to the end of the second chapter is foretold the punishment of the unbelieving Jews for their idolatrous practices, their confidence in their own strength, and distrust of God's protection; and moreover the destruction of idolatry, in consequence of the establishment of Messiah's kingdom. The whole of the third chapter, with the first verse of the fourth, is a prophecy of the calamities of the Babylonian invasion and captivity; with a particular amplification of the distress of the proud and luxurious daughters of Sion; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.2-Isa.4.6">Isa 4:2-6</reference> promises to the remnant, which shall have escaped this severe purgation, a future restoration to the favor and protection of God. <div eID="gen26472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26473" type="x-p"/> This prophecy was probably delivered in the time of Jotham, or perhaps in that of Uzziah, as Isaiah is said to have prophesied in his reign; to which time not any of his prophecies is so applicable as that of these chapters. The seventh verse of the second, and the latter part of the third chapter, plainly point out times in which riches abounded, and luxury and delicacy prevailed. Plenty of silver and gold could only arise from their commerce; particularly from that part of it which was carried on by the Red Sea. This circumstance seems to confine the prophecy within the limits above mentioned, while the port of Elath was in their hands; it was lost under Ahaz, and never recovered.
entries.1624bdc31f02e85c2c7a28908c39aae8bbf62057: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen26473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26474" type="x-p"/> In the last days "In the latter days" - "Wherever the latter times are mentioned in Scripture, the days of the Messiah are always meant," says Kimchi on this place: and, in regard to this place, nothing can be more clear and certain. And the mountain of the Lord's house, says the same author, is Mount Moriah, on which the temple was built. The prophet Micah, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.1-Mic.4.4">Mic 4:1-4</reference>, has repeated this prophecy of the establishment of the kingdom of Christ, and of its progress to universality and perfection, in the same words, with little and hardly any material variation: for as he did not begin to prophesy till Jotham's time, and this seems to be one of the first of Isaiah's prophecies, I suppose Micah to have taken it from hence. The variations, as I said, are of no great importance. <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Isa 2:2</reference>. הוא hu, after ונשא venissa, a word of some emphasis, may be supplied from Micah, if dropped in Isaiah. An ancient MS. has it here in the margin. It has in like manner been lost in <reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Isa 53:4</reference> (note), and in <reference osisRef="Psa.22.29">Psa 22:29</reference>, where it is supplied by the Syriac, and Septuagint. Instead of כל הגוים col haggoyim, all the nations, Micah has only עמים ammim, peoples; where the Syriac has כל עמים col ammim, all peoples, as probably it ought to be. <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa 2:3</reference>. For the second אל el, read ואל veel, seventeen MSS., one of my own, ancient, two editions, the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Chaldee, and so Micah, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.2">Mic 4:2</reference>. <reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Isa 2:4</reference>. Micah adds עד רחק ad rachok, afar off, which the Syriac also reads in this parallel place of Isaiah. It is also to be observed that Micah has improved the passage by adding a verse, or sentence, (<reference osisRef="Mic.4.4">Mic 4:4</reference>) for imagery and expression worthy even of the elegance of Isaiah: - "And they shall sit every man under his vine, <div eID="gen26474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26475" type="x-p"/> And under his fig tree, and none shall affright them: <div eID="gen26475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26476" type="x-p"/> For the mouth of Jehovah, God of hosts, hath spoken it." <div eID="gen26476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26477" type="x-p"/> The description of well established peace, by the image of "beating their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into pruning-hooks," is very poetical. The Roman poets have employed the same image, Martial, 14:34. "Falx ex ense." "Pax me certa ducis placidos curvavit in usus: <div eID="gen26477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26478" type="x-p"/> Agricolae nunc sum; militis ante fui." "Sweet peace has transformed me. I was once the property of the soldier, and am now the property of the husbandman." <div eID="gen26478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26479" type="x-p"/> The prophet Joel, <reference osisRef="Joe.3.10">Joe 3:10</reference>, hath reversed it, and applied it to war prevailing over peace: - "Beat your ploughshares into swords, <div eID="gen26479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26480" type="x-p"/> And your pruning-hooks into spears." <div eID="gen26480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26481" type="x-p"/> And so likewise the Roman poets: - - Non ullus aratro <div eID="gen26481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26482" type="x-p"/> Dignus honos: squalent abductis arva colonis, <div eID="gen26482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26483" type="x-p"/> Et curvae rigidum falces conflantur in ensem. <div eID="gen26483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26484" type="x-p"/> Virg., Georg. 1:506. "Agriculture has now no honor: the husbandmen being taken away to the wars, the fields are overgrown with weeds, and the crooked sickles are straightened into swords." <div eID="gen26484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26485" type="x-p"/> Bella diu tenuere viros: erat aptior ensis <div eID="gen26485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26486" type="x-p"/> Vomere: cedebat taurus arator equo <div eID="gen26486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26487" type="x-p"/> Sarcula cessabant; versique in pila ligones; <div eID="gen26487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26488" type="x-p"/> Factaque de rastri pondere cassis erat. <div eID="gen26488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26489" type="x-p"/> Ovid, Fast. 1:697. "War has lasted long, and the sword is preferred to the plough. The bull has given place to the war-horse; the weeding-hooks to pikes; and the harrow-pins have been manufactured into helmets." <div eID="gen26489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26490" type="x-p"/> The prophet Ezekiel, <reference osisRef="Eze.17.22-Eze.17.24">Eze 17:22-24</reference>, has presignified the same great event with equal clearness, though in a more abstruse form, in an allegory; from an image, suggested by the former part of the prophecy, happily introduced, and well pursued: - "Thus saith the Lord Jehovah: <div eID="gen26490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26491" type="x-p"/> I myself will take from the shoot of the lofty cedar, <div eID="gen26491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26492" type="x-p"/> Even a tender scion from the top of his scions will I pluck off: <div eID="gen26492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26493" type="x-p"/> And I myself will plant it on a mountain high and eminent. <div eID="gen26493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26494" type="x-p"/> On the lofty mountain of Israel will I plant it; <div eID="gen26494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26495" type="x-p"/> And it shall exalt its branch, and bring forth fruit, <div eID="gen26495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26496" type="x-p"/> And it shall become a majestic cedar: <div eID="gen26496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26497" type="x-p"/> And under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing; <div eID="gen26497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26498" type="x-p"/> In the shadow of its branches shall they dwell: <div eID="gen26498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26499" type="x-p"/> And all the trees of the field shall know, <div eID="gen26499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26500" type="x-p"/> That I Jehovah have brought low the high tree; <div eID="gen26500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26501" type="x-p"/> Have exalted the low tree; <div eID="gen26501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26502" type="x-p"/> Have dried up the green tree; <div eID="gen26502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26503" type="x-p"/> And have made the dry tree to flourish: <div eID="gen26503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26504" type="x-p"/> I Jehovah have spoken it, and will do it." <div eID="gen26504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26505" type="x-p"/> The word ונתתי venathatti, in this passage, <reference osisRef="Eze.17.22">Eze 17:22</reference>, as the sentence now stands, appears incapable of being reduced to any proper construction or sense. None of the ancient versions acknowledge it, except Theodotion, and the Vulgate; and all but the latter vary very much from the present reading of this clause. Houbigant's correction of the passage, by reading instead of ונתתי venathatti, ויונקת veyoneketh, and a tender scion which is not very unlike it, perhaps better ויונק veyonek, with which the adjective רך rach will agree without alteration - is ingenious and probable; and I have adopted it in the above translation. - L.
entries.98a2f2232056bcd18324b0f85cda0a66e914d114: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen26505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26506" type="x-p"/> To the house - The conjunction ו vau is added by nineteen of Kennicott's, thirteen of De Rossi's MSS., one of my own, and two editions, the Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, Arabic, and some copies of the Targum; And to the house. It makes the sentence more emphatic. <div eID="gen26506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26507" type="x-p"/> He will teach us of his ways - Unless God grant a revelation of his will, what can we know? <div eID="gen26507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26508" type="x-p"/> We will walk in his paths - Unless we purpose to walk in the light, of what use can that light be to us? <div eID="gen26508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26509" type="x-p"/> For out of Zion shall go forth the law - In the house of God, and in his ordinances only can we expect to hear the pure doctrines of revelation preached. <div eID="gen26509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26510" type="x-p"/> 1. God alone can give a revelation of his own will. <div eID="gen26510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26511" type="x-p"/> 2. We must use the proper means in order to know this will. <div eID="gen26511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26512" type="x-p"/> 3. We should know it in order to do it. <div eID="gen26512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26513" type="x-p"/> 4. We should do it in order to profit by it. <div eID="gen26513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26514" type="x-p"/> 5. He who will not walk in the light when God vouchsafes it, shall be shut up in everlasting darkness. <div eID="gen26514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26515" type="x-p"/> 6. Every man should help his neighbor to attain that light, life, and felicity: "Come ye, and let us walk in the light of the Lord."
entries.2353639cf88aedbaf4630a2af5b6afea0e8194d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen26515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26516" type="x-p"/> Neither shall they learn war any more - If wars are necessary, how deep must that fall be that renders them so! But what a reproach to humanity is the trade of war! Men are regularly instructed in it, as in any of the necessary arts. "How to dislodge most souls from their frail shrines <div eID="gen26516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26517" type="x-p"/> By bomb, sword, ball, and bayonet, is the art <div eID="gen26517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26518" type="x-p"/> Which some call great and glorious!" <div eID="gen26518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26519" type="x-p"/> And is this a necessary part of a finished education in civilized society? O Earth! Earth! Earth!
entries.eeda18aa17a2bc2972b513ff943e687dd6fe4de9: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen26519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26520" type="x-p"/> They be replenished "And they multiply" - Seven MSS. and one edition, for ישפיקו yaspiku, read ישפיחו yaspichu, "and have joined themselves to the children of strangers;" that is, in marriage or worship. - Dr. Jubb. So Vulg., adhaeserunt. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.1">Isa 14:1</reference>. But the very learned professor Chevalier Michaelis has explained the word יספחו yesupachu, <reference osisRef="Job.30.7">Job 30:7</reference>, (German translation, note on the place), in another manner; which perfectly well agrees with that place, and perhaps will be found to give as good a sense here. ספיח saphiach, the noun, means corn springing up, not from the seed regularly sown on cultivated land, but in the untilled field, from the scattered grains of the former harvest. This, by an easy metaphor, is applied to a spurious brood of children irregularly and casually begotten. The Septuagint seem to have understood the verb here in this sense, reading it as the Vulgate seems to have done. This justifies their version, which it is hard to account for in any other manner: και τεκνα πολλα αλλοφυλα εγενηθῃ αυτοις. Compare <reference osisRef="Hos.5.7">Hos 5:7</reference>, and the Septuagint there. But instead of ובילדי ubeyaldey, "and in the children," two of Kennicott's and eight of De Rossi's MSS. have וכילדי ucheyaldey, "and as the children." And they sin impudently as the children of strangers. See De Rossi. <div eID="gen26520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26521" type="x-p"/> And are soothsayers "They are filled with diviners" - Hebrews "They are filled from the east;" or "more than the east." The sentence is manifestly imperfect.
