The Septuagint, Vulgate, and Chaldee, seem to have read כמקדם kemikkedem; and the latter, with another word before it, signifying idols; "they are filled with idols as from of old." Houbigant, for מקדם mikkedem, reads מקסם mikkesem, as Brentius had proposed long ago. I rather think that both words together give us the true reading: מקדם mikkedem, מקסם mikkesem, "with divination from the east;" and that the first word has been by mistake omitted, from its similitude to the second.
entries.554cb9182dc97cec614e856ea84dc979561597c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen26521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26522" type="x-p"/> Their land is also full of horses "And his land is filled with horses" - This was in direct contradiction to God's command in the law: "But he (the king) shall not multiply horses to himself; nor cause the people to return to Egypt, to the end that he should multiply horses; neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold," <reference osisRef="Deu.17.16">Deu 17:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.17.17">Deu 17:17</reference>. Uzziah seems to have followed the example of Solomon, see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.26-1Kgs.10.29">1Kgs 10:26-29</reference>, who first transgressed in these particulars; he recovered the port of Elath on the Red Sea, and with it that commerce which in Solomon's days had "made silver and gold as plenteous at Jerusalem as stones," <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.15">2Chr 1:15</reference>. He had an army of 307,500 men, in which, as we may infer from the testimony of Isaiah, the chariots and horse made a considerable part. "The law above mentioned was to be a standing trial of prince and people, whether they had trust and confidence in God their deliverer." See Bp. Sherlock's Discourses on Prophecy. Dissert. iv., where he has excellently explained the reason and effect of the law, and the influence which the observance or neglect of it had on the affairs of the Israelites.
entries.33eb2879d7d403addaaf81f4f764986e36ee03de: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen26522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26523" type="x-p"/> Their land also is full of idols "And his land is filled with idols" - Uzziah and Fotham are both said, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.3">2Kgs 15:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.4">2Kgs 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.34">2Kgs 15:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.35">2Kgs 15:35</reference>, "to have done that which was right in the sight of the Lord;" that is, to have adhered to and maintained the legal worship of God, in opposition to idolatry and all irregular worship; for to this sense the meaning of that phrase is commonly to be restrained; "save that the high places were not removed where the people still sacrificed and burned incense." There was hardly any time when they were quite free from this irregular and unlawful practice, which they seem to have looked upon as very consistent with the true worship of God; and which seems in some measure to have been tolerated, while the tabernacle was removed from place to place, and before the temple was built. Even after the conversion of Manasseh, when he had removed the strange gods, commanded Judah to serve Jehovah the God of Israel, it is added, "Nevertheless the people did sacrifice still on the high places, yet unto Jehovah their God only," <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.17">2Chr 33:17</reference>. The worshipping on the high places therefore does not necessarily imply idolatry; and from what is said of these two kings, Uzziah and Jotham, we may presume that the public exercise of idolatrous worship was not permitted in their time. The idols therefore here spoken of must have been such as were designed for a private and secret use. Such probably were the teraphim so often mentioned in Scripture; a kind of household gods, of human form, as it should seem, (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.13">1Sam 19:13</reference> (note), and compare <reference osisRef="Gen.31.34">Gen 31:34</reference> (note)), of different magnitude, used for idolatrous and superstitious purposes, particularly for divination, and as oracles, which they consulted for direction in their affairs.
entries.bc7b6e5d4f773af8ae494b4c7e6914147e37df4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen26523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26524" type="x-p"/> Boweth down "Shall be bowed down" - This has reference to the preceding verse. They bowed themselves down to their idols, therefore shall they be bowed down and brought low under the avenging hand of God. <div eID="gen26524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26525" type="x-p"/> Therefore forgive them not - "And thou wilt not forgive them." - L.
entries.742cd3ae328081ef8ab7d149717ec7eeb31a486f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> "When he ariseth to strike the earth with terror" - On the authority of the Septuagint, confirmed by the Arabic and an ancient MS., I have added here to the text a line, which in the 19th and 21st verses (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.19">Isa 2:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.21">Isa 2:21</reference>) is repeated together with the preceding line, and has, I think, evidently been omitted by mistake in this place. The MS. here varies only in one letter from the reading of the other two verses; it has בארץ baarets, instead of הארץ haarets. None of De Rossi's MSS. confirm this addition. The line added is, When he ariseth to strike the earth with terror.
entries.ec47e5c939fb0f965c8218978777316d6bc4dfef: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen26525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26526" type="x-p"/> Be humbled - "שפל ושח shaphel veshach, read שפלו שח shaphelu shach." - Dr. Durell. Which rectifies the grammatical construction. No MS. or version confirms this reading.
entries.59b85fd66f369e84aac870630b2de9d32b8e8aa6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen26526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26527" type="x-p"/> And upon all the cedars "Even against all the cedars" - Princes, potentates, rulers, captains, rich men, etc. - So Kimchi. These verses afford us a striking example of that peculiar way of writing, which makes a principal characteristic of the parabolical or poetical style of the Hebrews, and in which the prophets deal so largely, namely, their manner of exhibiting things Divine, spiritual, moral, and political, by a set of images taken from things natural, artificial, religious, historical, in the way of metaphor or allegory. Of these nature furnishes much the largest and the most pleasing share; and all poetry has chiefly recourse to natural images, as the richest and most powerful source of illustration. But it may be observed of the Hebrew poetry in particular, that in the use of such images, and in the application of them in the way of illustration and ornament, it is more regular and constant than any other poetry whatever; that it has for the most part a set of images appropriated in a manner to the explication of certain subjects. Thus you will find, in many other places besides this before us, that cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan, are used in the way of metaphor and allegory for kings, princes, potentates of the highest rank; high mountains and lofty hills, for kingdoms, republics, states, cities; towers and fortresses, for defenders and protectors, whether by counsel or strength, in peace or war; ships of Tarshish and works of art, and invention employed in adorning them, for merchants, men enriched by commerce, and abounding in all the luxuries and elegances of life, such as those of Tyre and Sidon; for it appears from the course of the whole passage, and from the train of ideas, that the fortresses and the ships are to be taken metaphorically, as well as the high trees and the lofty mountains. <div eID="gen26527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26528" type="x-p"/> Ships of Tarshish - Are in Scripture frequently used by a metonymy for ships in general, especially such as are employed in carrying on traffic between distant countries, as Tarshish was the most celebrated mart of those times, frequented of old by the Phoenicians, and the principal source of wealth to Judea and the neighboring countries. The learned seem now to be perfectly well agreed that Tarshish is Tartessus, a city of Spain, at the mouth of the river Baetis, whence the Phoenicians, who first opened this trade, brought silver and gold, (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.9">Jer 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.27.12">Eze 27:12</reference>), in which that country then abounded; and, pursuing their voyage still farther to the Cassiterides, (Bogart, Canaan, 1 c. 39; Huet, Hist. de Commerce, p. 194), the islands of Scilly and Cornwall, they brought from thence lead and tin. <div eID="gen26528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26529" type="x-p"/> Tarshish is celebrated in Scripture, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.17">2Chr 8:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.18">2Chr 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.21">2Chr 9:21</reference>, for the trade which Solomon carried on thither, in conjunction with the Tyrians. Jehoshaphat, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.48">1Kgs 22:48</reference>;<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.36">2Chr 20:36</reference>, attempted afterwards to renew their trade. And from the account given of his attempt it appears that his fleet was to sail to Ezion-geber on the Red Sea; they must therefore have designed to sail round Africa, as Solomon's fleet had done before, (see Huet, Histoire de Commerce, p. 32), for it was a three years' voyage, (<reference osisRef="2Chr.9.21">2Chr 9:21</reference>), and they brought gold from Ophir, probably on the coast of Arabia; silver from Tartessus; and ivory, apes, and peacocks, from Africa." אופרי Afri, Africa, the Roman termination, Africa terra. תרשיש Tarshish, some city or country in Africa. So the Chaldee on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.49">1Kgs 22:49</reference>, where it renders תרשיש Tarshish by אפריקה Aphricah; and compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.36">2Chr 20:36</reference>, from whence it appears, to go to Ophir and to Tarshish is one and the same thing." - Dr. Jubb. <div eID="gen26529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26530" type="x-p"/> It is certain that under Pharaoh Necho, about two hundred years afterwards, this voyage was made by the Egyptians; Herodot. 4:42. They sailed from the Red Sea, and returned by the Mediterranean, and they performed it in three years, just the same time that the voyage under Solomon had taken up. It appears likewise from Pliny, Nat. Hist., 2:67, that the passage round the Cape of Good Hope was known and frequently practiced before his time, by Hanno, the Carthaginian, when Carthage was in its glory; by one Eudoxus, in the time of Ptolemy Lathyrus, king of Egypt; and Coelus Antipater, a historian of good credit, somewhat earlier than Pliny, testifies that he had seen a merchant who had made the voyage from Gades to Ethiopia. The Portuguese under Vasco de Gama, near three hundred years ago, recovered this navigation, after it had been intermitted and lost for many centuries. - L.
entries.f0337b38b8dc7a68cb5c4c7bde3711c814345c7a: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen26530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26531" type="x-p"/> Shall utterly abolish "Shall disappear" - The ancient versions and an ancient MS. read יחלפו yachalpu, plural. One of my MSS. reads יחלוף yachaloph, probably a mistake for יחלפו yachalpu.
entries.74e117866dbc3bdf78f02ae06a0f002f22fe9627: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen26531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26532" type="x-p"/> Into the holes of the rocks "Into caverns of rocks" - The country of Judea being mountainous and rocky, is full of caverns, as appears from the history of David's persecution under Saul. At En-gedi, in particular, there was a cave so large that David with six hundred men hid themselves in the sides of it; and Saul entered the mouth of the cave without perceiving that any one was there, 1 Samuel 24. Josephus, Antiq., lib. xiv., c. 15, and Bell. Jud., lib. 1, c. 16, tells us of a numerous gang of banditti, who, having infested the country, and being pursued by Herod with his army retired into certain caverns almost inaccessible, near Arbela in Galilee, where they were with great difficulty subdued. Some of these were natural, others artificial. "Beyond Damascus," says Strabo, lib. xvi., "are two mountains called Trachones, from which the country has the name of Trachonitis; and from hence towards Arabia and Iturea, are certain rugged mountains, in which there are deep caverns, one of which will hold four thousand men." Tavernier, Voyage de Perse, part ii., chap. 4, speaks of a grot, between Aleppo and Bir, that would hold near three thousand horse. "Three hours distant from Sidon, about a mile from the sea, there runs along a high rocky mountain, in the sides of which are hewn a multitude of grots, all very little differing from each other. They have entrances about two feet square: on the inside you find in most or all of them a room of about four yards square. There are of these subterraneous caverns two hundred in number. It may, with probability at least, be concluded that these places were contrived for the use of the living, and not of the dead. Strabo describes the habitations of the Troglodytae to have been somewhat of this kind." - Maundrell, p. 118. The Horites, who dwelt in Mount Seir, were Troglodytae, as their name הרים horim, imports. But those mentioned by Strabo were on each side of the Arabian gulf. Mohammed (Koran, chap. 15 xxvi.) speaks of a tribe of Arabians, the tribe of Thamud, "who hewed houses out of the mountains, to secure themselves." Thus, "because of the Midianites, the children of Israel made them the dens which are in the mountains, and caves and strong holds," <reference osisRef="Jdg.6.2">Jdg 6:2</reference>. To these they betook themselves for refuge in times of distress and hostile invasion: "When the men of Israel saw that they were in a strait, for the people were distressed, then the people did hide themselves in caves, and in thickets, and in rocks, and in high places, and in pits," <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.6">1Sam 13:6</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Jer.41.9">Jer 41:9</reference>. Therefore "to enter into the rock, to go into the holes of the rocks, and into the caves of the earth," was to them a very proper and familiar image to express terror and consternation. The prophet Hosea, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.8">Hos 10:8</reference>, hath carried the same image farther, and added great strength and spirit to it: "They shall say to the mountains, Cover us; <div eID="gen26532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26533" type="x-p"/> And to the hills, Fall on us;" which image, together with these of Isaiah, is adopted by the sublime author of the Revelation, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev 6:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Rev 6:16</reference>, who frequently borrows his imagery from our prophet. - L.
entries.1eaca0da3a401a7f6184b985bad4bb9e38deff0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen26533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26534" type="x-p"/> Which they made each one for himself to worship "Which they have made to worship" - The word לו lo, for himself, is omitted by two ancient MSS., and is unnecessary. It does not appear that any copy of the Septuagint has it, except MS. Pachom, and MS. 1. D. II., and they have ἑαυτοις, להם lahem, to themselves. <div eID="gen26534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26535" type="x-p"/> To the moles - They shall carry their idols with them into the dark caverns, old ruins, or desolate places, to which they shall flee for refuge; and so shall give them up, and relinquish them to the filthy animals that frequent such places, and have taken possession of them as their proper habitation. Bellonias, Greaves, P. Lucas, and many other travelers, speak of bats of an enormous size, as inhabiting the Great Pyramid. See Harmer, Obs., vol. ii., 455. Three MSS. express חפרפרות chapharperoth, the moles as one word.
entries.db1cdf80ff9b69ae45b60923c1e7fdee0bbfee7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen26535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26536" type="x-p"/> Cease ye from man - Trust neither in him, nor in the gods that he has invented. Neither he, nor they, can either save or destroy.  <chapter eID="Isa.2"/> <div eID="gen26536" type="x-p"/>

entries.3611c3c92c3e6be9439bafb81671c4dcc3b186cb: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.1">Isa 2:1</reference> <div eID="gen12811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12812" type="x-p"/> The limits of this address are very obvious. The end of <reference osisRef="Isa.4.1-Isa.4.6">Isa 4:1-6</reference> connects itself with the beginning of chapter 2, so as to form a circle. After various alternations of admonition, reproach, and threatening, the prophet reaches at last the object of the promise with which he started. Chapter 5, on the other hand, commences afresh with a parable. It forms an independent address, although it is included, along with the previous chapters, under the heading in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.1">Isa 2:1</reference> : <hi type="italic">“The word which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw over Judah and Jerusalem.”</hi> Chapters 2-5 may have existed under this heading before the whole collection arose. It was then adopted in this form into the general collection, so as to mark the transition from the prologue to the body of the book. The prophet describes what he here says concerning Judah and Jerusalem as <hi type="italic">“the word which he saw.”</hi> When men speak to one another, the words are not seen, but heard. But when God spoke to the prophet, it was in a supersensuous way, and the prophet saw it. The mind indeed has no more eyes than ears; but a mind qualified to perceive what is supersensuous is altogether eye. <div eID="gen12812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12813" type="x-p"/> The manner in which Isaiah commences this second address is altogether unparalleled. There is no other example of a prophecy beginning with והיה. And it is very easy to discover the reason why. The <hi type="italic">praet. consecutivum</hi> <hi type="italic">v'hâyâh</hi> derives the force of a future from the context alone; whereas the <hi type="italic">fut. consecutivum</hi> <hi type="italic">vay'hi</hi> (with which historical books and sections very generally commence) is shown to be an aorist by its simple form. Moreover, the <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> in the <hi type="italic">fut. consecut.</hi> has almost entirely lost its copulative character; in the <hi type="italic">praet. consec.</hi>, on the other hand, it retains it with all the greater force. The prophet therefore commences with “and”; and it is from what follows, not from what goes before, that we learn that <hi type="italic">hayah</hi> is used in a future sense. But this is not the only strange thing. It is also an unparalleled occurrence, for a prophetic address, which runs as this does through all the different phases of the prophetic discourses generally (viz., exhortation, reproof, threatening, and promise), to commence with a promise. We are in a condition, however, to explain the cause of this remarkable phenomenon with certainty, and not merely to resort to conjecture. <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Isa 2:2-4</reference> do not contain Isaiah’s own words, but the words of another prophet taken out of their connection. We find them again in Mic 4:1-4; and whether Isaiah took them from Micah, or whether both Isaiah and Micah took them from some common source, in either case they were not originally Isaiah's.<note placement="foot">The historical statement in <reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jer 26:18</reference>, from which we learn that it was in the days of Hezekiah that Micah uttered the threat contained in Mic 3:12 (of which the promise sin Mic 4:1-4 and <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Isa 2:2-4</reference> are the direct antithesis), apparently precludes the idea that Isaiah borrowed from Micah, whilst the opposite is altogether inadmissible, for reasons assigned above. Ewald and Hitzig have therefore come to the conclusion, quite independently of each other, that both Micah and Isaiah repeated the words of a third and earlier prophet, most probably of Joel. And the passage in question has really very much in common with the book of Joel, viz., the idea of the melting down of ploughshares and pruning-hooks (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.10">Joe 3:10</reference>), the combination of <hi type="italic">râb</hi> (many) and <hi type="italic">âtsum</hi> (strong), of <hi type="italic">gephen</hi> (vine) and <hi type="italic">te'enah</hi> (fig-tree), as compared with Mic 4:4; also the attesting formula, “For Jehovah hath spoken it” (<hi type="italic">Chi</hi> <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> <hi type="italic">dibber</hi>: <reference osisRef="Joel.3.8">Joe 3:8</reference>), which is not found in Micah, whereas it is very common in Isaiah - a fact which makes the sign itself a very feeble one (cf., 1Ki 14:11, also Oba 1:18). Hitzig, indeed, maintains that it is only by restoring this passage that the prophetic writings of Joel receive their proper rounding off and an appropriate termination; but although swords and spears beaten into ploughshares and pruning-hooks form a good antithesis to ploughshares and pruning-hooks beaten into swords and spears (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.10">Joe 3:10</reference>), the coming of great and mighty nations to Mount Zion after the previous judgment of extermination would be too unprepared or much too abrupt a phenomenon. On the other hand, we cannot admit the force of the arguments adduced either by E. Meier (<hi type="italic">Joel,</hi> p. 195) or by Knobel and G. Baur (<hi type="italic">Amos</hi>, p. 29) against the authorship of Joel, which rest upon a misapprehension of the meaning of Joel’s prophecies, which the former regards as too full of storm and battle, the latter as too exclusive and one-sided, for Joel to be the author of the passage in question. At the same time, we would call attention to the fact, that the promises in Micah form the obverse side to the previous threatenings of judgment, so that there is a presumption of their originality; also that the passage contains as many traces of Micah’s style (see above at <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa 1:3</reference>) as we could expect to find in these three verses; and, as we shall show at the conclusion of this cycle of predictions (chapters 1-6), that the historical fact mentioned in <reference osisRef="Jer.26.18">Jer 26:18</reference> may be reconciled in the simplest possible manner with the assumption that Isaiah borrowed these words of promise from Micah. (See Caspari, <hi type="italic">Micha</hi>, p. 444ff.)</note> <div eID="gen12813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12814" type="x-p"/> Nor was it even intended that they should appear to be his. Isaiah has not fused them into the general flow of his own prophecy, as the prophets usually do with the predictions of their predecessors. He does not reproduce them, but, as we may observe from the abrupt commencement, he quote them. It is true, this hardly seems to tally with the heading, which describes what follows as the word of Jehovah which Isaiah saw. But the discrepancy is only an apparent one. It was the spirit of prophecy, which called to Isaiah’s remembrance a prophetic saying that had already been uttered, and made it the starting-point of the thoughts which followed in Isaiah’s mind. The borrowed promise is not introduced for its own sake, but is simply a self-explaining introduction to the exhortations and threatenings which follow, and through which the prophet works his way to a conclusion of his own, that is closely intertwined with the borrowed commencement.
entries.5924aa1b26e326e28cebf69f566d541121dbfccb: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Isa 2:2</reference> <div eID="gen12814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12815" type="x-p"/> The subject of the borrowed prophecy is Israel’s future glory: <hi type="italic">“And it cometh to pass at the end of the days, the mountain of the house of Jehovah will be set at the top of the mountains, and exalted over hills; and all nations pour unto it.”</hi> The expression “the last days” (<hi type="italic">acharith</hi> <hi type="italic">hayyamim</hi>, “the end of the days”), which does not occur anywhere else in Isaiah, is always used in an eschatological sense. It never refers to the course of history immediately following the time being, but invariably indicates the furthest point in the history of this life - the point which lies on the outermost limits of the speaker’s horizon. This horizon was a very fluctuating one. The history of prophecy is just the history of its gradual extension, and of the filling up of the intermediate space. In Jacob’s blessing (Gen 49) the conquest of the land stood in the foreground of the <hi type="italic">acharith</hi> or last days, and the perspective was regulated accordingly. But here in Isaiah the <hi type="italic">acharith</hi> contained no such mixing together of events belonging to the more immediate and the most distant future. It was therefore the last time in its most literal and purest sense, commencing with the beginning of the New Testament aeon, and terminating at its close (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">Heb 1:1</reference>; 1Pe 1:20, with 1 Cor 15 and the Revelation). The prophet here predicted that the mountain which bore the temple of Jehovah, and therefore was already in dignity the most exalted of all mountains, would. one day tower in actual height above all the high places of the earth. The basaltic mountains of Bashan, which rose up in bold peaks and columns, might now look down with scorn and contempt upon the small limestone hill which Jehovah had chosen (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.16-Ps.68.17">Psa 68:16-17</reference>); but this was an incongruity which the last times would remove, by making the outward correspond to the inward, the appearance to the reality and the intrinsic worth. That this is the prophet’s meaning is confirmed by <reference osisRef="Ezek.40.2">Eze 40:2</reference>, where the temple mountain looks gigantic to the prophet, and also by Zec 14:10, where all Jerusalem is described as towering above the country round about, which would one day become a plain. The question how this can possibly take place in time, since it presupposes a complete subversion of the whole of the existing order of the earth’s surface, is easily answered. The prophet saw the new Jerusalem of the last days on this side, and the new Jerusalem of the new earth on the other (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.10">Rev 21:10</reference>), blended as it were together, and did not distinguish the one from the other. But whilst we thus avoid all unwarrantable spiritualizing, it still remains a question what meaning the prophet attached to the word <hi type="italic">b'rosh</hi> (<hi type="italic">“at the top”</hi>). Did he mean that Moriah would one day stand <hi type="italic">upon the top</hi> of the mountains that surrounded it (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.16">Psa 72:16</reference>), or that it would stand <hi type="italic">at their head</hi> (as in 1Ki 21:9, 1Ki 21:12; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.7">Amo 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.7">Jer 31:7</reference>)? The former is Hofmann’s view, as given in his <hi type="italic">Weissagung und Erfüllung</hi>, ii. 217: “he did not indeed mean that the mountains would be piled up one upon the other, and the temple mountain upon the top, but that the temple mountain would appear to float upon the summit of the others.” But as the expression <hi type="italic">“will be set”</hi> (<hi type="italic">nacon</hi>) does not favour this apparently romantic exaltation, and <hi type="italic">b'rosh</hi> occurs more frequently in the sense of <hi type="italic">“at the head”</hi> than in that of <hi type="italic">“on the top,”</hi> I decide for my own part in favour of the second view, though I agree so far with Hofmann, that it is not merely an exaltation of the temple mountain in the estimation of the nations that is predicted, but a physical and external elevation also. And when thus outwardly exalted, the divinely chosen mountain would become the rendezvous and centre of unity for all nations. They would all “flow unto it” (<hi type="italic">nâhar</hi>, a denom. verb, from <hi type="italic">nâhâr</hi>, a river, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.51.44">Jer 51:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.12">Jer 31:12</reference>). It is the temple of Jehovah which, being thus rendered visible to nations afar off, exerts such magnetic attraction, and with such success. Just as at a former period men had been separated and estranged from one another in the plain of Shinar, and thus different nations had first arisen; so would the nations at a future period assemble together on the mountain of the house of Jehovah, and there, as members of one family, live together in amity again. And as Babel (<hi type="italic">confusion</hi>, as its name signifies) was the place whence the stream of nations poured into all the world; so would Jerusalem (the <hi type="italic">city of peace</hi>) become the place into which the stream of nations would empty itself, and where all would be reunited once more. At the present time there was only one people, viz., Israel, which made pilgrimages to Zion on the great festivals, but it would be very different then.
entries.cd784090fa2de9a84dc8f45953a0255d5623dae5: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa 2:3</reference> <hi type="italic">“And peoples in multitude go and say, Come, let us go up to the mountain of Jehovah, to the house of the God of Jacob; let Him instruct us out of His ways, and we will walk in His paths.”</hi> This is their signal for starting, and their song by the way (cf., Zec 8:21-22). What urges them on is the desire for salvation. Desire for salvation expresses itself in the name they give to the point towards which they are travelling: they call Moriah “the mountain of Jehovah,” and the temple upon it “the house of the God of Jacob.” Through frequent use, <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> had become the popular name for the people of God; but the name they employ is the choicer name <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi>, which is the name of affection in the mouth of Micah, of whose style we are also reminded by the expression “many peoples” (<hi type="italic">ammim</hi> <hi type="italic">rabbim</hi>). Desire for salvation expresses itself in the object of their journey; they wish Jehovah to teach them <hi type="italic">“out of His ways,”</hi> - a rich source of instruction with which they desire to be gradually entrusted. The preposition <hi type="italic">min</hi> (out of, or from) is not partitive here, but refers, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.94.12">Psa 94:12</reference>, to the source of instruction. The “ways of Jehovah” are the ways which God Himself takes, and by which men are led by Him - the revealed ordinances of His will and action. Desire for salvation also expresses itself in the resolution with which they set out: they not only wish to learn, but are resolved to act according to what they learn. <hi type="italic">“We will walk in His paths:”</hi> the hortative is used here, as it frequently is (e.g., <reference osisRef="Gen.27.4">Gen 27:4</reference>, vid., Ges. §128, 1,<hi type="italic">c</hi>), to express either the subjective intention or subjective conclusion. The words supposed to be spoken by the multitude of heathen going up to Zion terminate here. The prophet then adds the reason and object of this holy pilgrimage of the nations: <hi type="italic">“For instruction will go out from Zion, and the word of Jehovah from Jerusalem.”</hi> The principal emphasis is upon the expressions “from Zion” and “from Jerusalem.” It is a triumphant utterance of the sentiment that “salvation is of the Jews” (Joh 4:22). From Zion-Jerusalem there would go forth <hi type="italic">thorah</hi>, i.e., instruction as to the questions which man has to put to God, and <hi type="italic">debar</hi> <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, the word of Jehovah, which created the world at first, and by which it is spiritually created anew. Whatever promotes the true prosperity of the nations, comes from Zion-Jerusalem. There the nations assemble together; they take it thence to their own homes, and thus Zion-Jerusalem becomes the fountain of universal good. For from the time that Jehovah made choice of Zion, the holiness of Sinai was transferred to Zion (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference>), which now presented the same aspect as Sinai had formerly done, when God invested it with holiness by appearing there in the midst of myriads of angels. What had been commenced at Sinai for Israel, would be completed at Zion for all the world. This was fulfilled on that day of Pentecost, when the disciples, the first-fruits of the church of Christ, proclaimed the <hi type="italic">thorah</hi> of Zion, i.e., the gospel, in the languages of all the world. It was fulfilled, as Theodoret observes, in the fact that the word of the gospel, rising from Jerusalem “as from a fountain,” flowed through the whole of the known world. But these fulfilments were only preludes to a conclusion which is still to be looked for in the future. For what is promised in the following v. is still altogether unfulfilled.
entries.3da56f7f092832aca91417229dcee3dfe2996391: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.4">Isa 2:4</reference> <hi type="italic">“And He will judge between the nations, and deliver justice to many peoples; and they forge their swords into coulters, and their spears into pruning-hooks: nation lifts not up the sword against nation, neither do they exercise themselves in war any more.”</hi> Since the nations betake themselves in this manner as pupils to the God of revelation and the word of His revelation, He becomes the supreme judge and umpire among them. If any dispute arise, it is no longer settled by the compulsory force of war, but by the word of God, to which all bow with willing submission. With such power as this in the peace-sustaining word of God (Zec 9:10), there is no more need for weapons of iron: they are turned into the instruments of peaceful employment, into <hi type="italic">ittim</hi> (probably a synonym for <hi type="italic">ethim</hi> in <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.21">1Sa 13:21</reference>), plough-knives or coulters, which cut the furrows for the ploughshare to turn up and <hi type="italic">mazmeroth</hi>, bills or pruning-hooks, with which vines are pruned to increase their fruit-bearing power. There is also no more need for military practice, for there is no use in exercising one’s self in what cannot be applied. It is useless, and men dislike it. There is peace, not an armed peace, but a full, true, God-given and blessed peace. What even a Kant regarded as possible is now realized, and that not by the so-called Christian powers, but by the power of God, who favours the object for which an Elihu Burritt enthusiastically longs, rather than the politics of the Christian powers. It is in war that the power of the beast culminates in the history of the world. This beast will then be destroyed. The true humanity which sin has choked up will gain the mastery, and the world’s history will keep Sabbath. And may we not indulge the hope, on the ground of such prophetic words as these, that the history of the world will not terminate without having kept a Sabbath? Shall we correct Isaiah, according to Quenstedt, lest we should become chiliasts? “The humanitarian ideas of Christendom,” says a thoughtful Jewish scholar, “have their roots in the Pentateuch, and more especially in Deuteronomy. But in the prophets, particularly in Isaiah, they reach a height which will probably not be attained and fully realized by the modern world for centuries to come.” Yet they will be realized. What the prophetic words appropriated by Isaiah here affirm, is a moral postulate, the goal of sacred history, the predicted counsel of God.
entries.b966932b215a962f408599baa7edae23601a5344: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.5">Isa 2:5</reference> <div eID="gen12815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12816" type="x-p"/> Isaiah presents himself to his contemporaries with this older prophecy of the exalted and world-wide calling of the people of Jehovah, holds it up before them as a mirror, and exclaims in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.5">Isa 2:5</reference>, <hi type="italic">“O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of Jehovah.”</hi> This exhortation is formed under the influence of the context, from which <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Isa 2:2-4</reference> are taken, as we may see from Mic 4:5, and also of the quotation itself. The use of the term <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> is not indeed altogether strange to Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.17">Isa 8:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.20-Isa.10.21">Isa 10:20-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.23">Isa 29:23</reference>), but he prefers the use of <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.24">Isa 1:24</reference> with <reference osisRef="Gen.49.24">Gen 49:24</reference>).With the words “O house of Jacob” he now turns to his people, whom so glorious a future awaits, because Jehovah has made it the scene of His manifested presence and grace, and summons it to walk in the light of such a God, to whom all nations will press at the end of the days. The summons, “Come, let us walk,” is the echo of <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa 2:3</reference>, “Come, let us go;” and as Hitzig observes, “Isaiah endeavours, like Paul in <reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">Rom 11:14</reference>, to stir up his countrymen to a noble jealousy, by setting before them the example of the heathen.” The “light of Jehovah” (<hi type="italic">'or</hi> <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, in which the echo of <hi type="italic">v'yorenu</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa 2:3</reference> is hardly accidental; cf., <reference osisRef="Prov.6.23">Pro 6:23</reference>) is the knowledge of Jehovah Himself, as furnished by means of positive revelation, His manifested love. It was now high time to walk in the light of Jehovah, i.e., to turn this knowledge into life, and reciprocate this love; and it was especially necessary to exhort Israel to this, now that Jehovah had given up His people, just because in their perverseness they had done the very opposite. This mournful declaration, which the prophet was obliged to make in order to explain his warning cry, he changes into the form of a prayerful sigh.
entries.6adee3f7f58737ee745a3dad74ba460b8251343a: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Isa 2:6</reference> <hi type="italic">“For Thou hast rejected Thy people, the house of Jacob; for they are filled with things from the east, and are conjurors like the Philistines; and with the children of foreigners they go hand in hand.”</hi> Here again we have <hi type="italic">“for”</hi> (<hi type="italic">Chi</hi>) twice in succession; the first giving the reason for the warning cry, the second vindicating the reason assigned. The words are addressed to Jehovah, not to the people. Saad., Gecatilia, and Rashi adopt the rendering, “Thou has given up thy nationality;” and this rendering is supported by J. D. Michaelis, Hitzig, and Luzzatto. But the word means “people,” not “nationality;” and the rendering is inadmissible, and would never have been thought of were it not that there was apparently something strange in so sudden an introduction of an address to God. But in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.9">Isa 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Isa 9:2</reference>, and other passages, the prophecy takes the form of a prayer. And <hi type="italic">nâtash</hi> (cast off) with <hi type="italic">âm</hi> (people) for its object recals such passages as <reference osisRef="Ps.94.14">Psa 94:14</reference> and 1Sa 12:22. Jehovah had put away His people, i.e., rejected them, and left them to themselves, for the following reasons: (1.) Because they were “full from the east” (<hi type="italic">mikkedem</hi>: <hi type="italic">min</hi> denotes the source from which a person draws and fills himself, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.34">Jer 51:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.6">Eze 32:6</reference>), i.e., full of eastern manners and customs, more especially of idolatrous practices. By “the east” (<hi type="italic">kedem</hi>) we are to understand Arabia as far as the peninsula of Sinai, and also the Aramaean lands of the Euphrates. Under Uzziah and Jotham, whose sway extended to Elath, the seaport town of the Elanitic Gulf, the influence of the south-east predominated; but under Ahaz and Hezekiah, on account of their relations to Asshur, Aram, and Babylon, that of the north-east. The conjecture of Gesenius, that we should read <hi type="italic">mikkesem</hi>, i.e., of soothsaying, it a very natural one; but it obliterates without any necessity the name of the region from which Judah’s imitative propensities received their impulse and materials. (2.) They were <hi type="italic">onenim</hi> (= <hi type="italic">meonenim</hi>, Mic 5:11, from the <hi type="italic">poel onen</hi>: 2Ki 21:6), probably <hi type="italic">“cloud-gatherers”</hi> or <hi type="italic">“storm-raisers,”</hi><note placement="foot">There is no force in the explanation “concealing,” i.e., practising secret arts; for the meaning “cover” or “conceal” is arbitrarily transferred to the verb <hi type="italic">onen</hi>, from <hi type="italic">gânan</hi> and <hi type="italic">Cânan</hi>, which are supposed to be cognate roots. As a denominative of <hi type="italic">ânân</hi>, the cloud, however (on this name for the clouds, see at <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference>), <hi type="italic">onen</hi> might mean “he gathered auguries from the clouds.” Or if we take <hi type="italic">onen</hi> as a synonym of <hi type="italic">innen</hi> in <reference osisRef="Gen.9.14">Gen 9:14</reference>, it would mean “to raise storms,” which would give the rendering νεφοδιῶκται, <hi type="italic">tempestarii</hi>, storm-raisers. The derivation of <hi type="italic">onen</hi> from Ny(i, in the sense of the Arabic <hi type="italic">'âna</hi> (impf. <hi type="italic">ya ı̄nu</hi>), as it were to ogle, <hi type="italic">oculo maligno petere et fascinare</hi>, founders on <hi type="italic">annen</hi>, the word used in the Targums, which cannot possibly be traced to Ny(i. From a purely philological standpoint, however, there is still another explanation possible. From the idea of <hi type="italic">coming to meet</hi> we get the transitive meaning to hold back, shut in, or hinder, particularly to hold back a horse by the reins (<hi type="italic">inân</hi>), or when applied to sexual relations, <hi type="italic">'unna</hi> (<hi type="italic">'unnina</hi>, <hi type="italic">u'inna</hi>) )<hi type="italic">an el - mar'ati</hi>, “he is prevented (by magic) from approaching his wife,” Beside the Arabic <hi type="italic">'innı̄n</hi> and <hi type="italic">ma'nūn</hi> (to render sexually impotent by witchcraft), we find the Syriac <hi type="italic">'anono</hi> used in the same sense.</note><hi type="italic">like the Philistines</hi> (the people conquered by Uzziah, and then again by Hezekiah), among whom witchcraft was carried on in guilds, whilst a celebrated oracle of Baal-Zebub existed at Ekron. (3.) And they make common cause with children of foreigners. This is the explanation adopted by Gesenius, Knobel, and others. <hi type="italic">Sâphak</hi> with <hi type="italic">Cappaim</hi> signifies to <hi type="italic">clap hands</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job 27:23</reference>). The <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> followed by <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is only used here in the sense of <hi type="italic">striking hands with a person</hi>. Luzzatto explains it as meaning, “They find satisfaction in the children of foreigners; it is only through them that they are contented;” but this is contrary to the usage of the language, according to which <hi type="italic">hispik</hi> in post-biblical Hebrew signifies either suppeditare or (like <hi type="italic">saphak</hi> in 1Ki 20:10) <hi type="italic">sufficere</hi>. Jerome renders it <hi type="italic">pueris alienis adhaeserunt</hi>; but <hi type="italic">yalde</hi> <hi type="italic">nâc'rim</hi> does not mean <hi type="italic">pueri alieni</hi>, boys hired for licentious purposes, but the “sons of strangers” generally (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.10">Isa 60:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.5">Isa 61:5</reference>), with a strong emphasis upon their unsanctified birth, the heathenism inherited from their mother’s womb. With heathen by birth, the prophet would say, the people of Jehovah made common cause. <div eID="gen12816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12817" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.2.7">Isa 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.8">Isa 2:8</reference> he describes still further how the land of the people of Jehovah, in consequence of all this (on the future consec. see Ges. §129, 2, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), was crammed full of objects of luxury, of self-confidence, of estrangement from God: <hi type="italic">“And their land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end of their treasures; and their land is filled with horses, and there is no end of their chariots. And their land is filled with - idols; the work of their own hands they worship, that which their own fingers have made.”</hi> The glory of Solomon, which revived under Uzziah’s fifty-two years’ reign, and was sustained through Jotham’s reign of sixteen years, carried with it the curse of the law; for the law of the king, in Deu 17:14., prohibited the multiplying of horses, and also the accumulation of gold and silver. Standing armies, and stores of national treasures, like everything else which ministers to carnal self-reliance, were opposed to the spirit of the theocracy. Nevertheless Judaea was immeasurably full of such seductions to apostasy; and not of those alone, but also of things which plainly revealed it, viz., of <hi type="italic">elilim</hi>, idols (the same word is used in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.4">Lev 19:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.1">Lev 26:1</reference>, from <hi type="italic">elil</hi>, vain or worthless; it is therefore equivalent to “not-gods”). They worshipped the work of “their own” hands, what “their own” fingers had made: two distributive singulars, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">Isa 5:23</reference>, the hands and fingers of every individual (vid., Mic 5:12-13, where the idols are classified). The condition of the land, therefore, was not only opposed to the law of the king, but at variance with the decalogue also. The existing glory was the most offensive caricature of the glory promised to the nation; for the people, whose God was one day to become the desire and salvation of all nations, had exchanged Him for the idols of the nations, and was vying with them in the appropriation of heathen religion and customs.
entries.3c91d8d50ce73d4e93f374fec594f0a85431adef: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.9-Isa.2.11">Isa 2:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen12817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12818" type="x-p"/> It was a state ripe for judgment, from which, therefore, the prophet could at once proceed, without any further preparation, to the proclamation of judgment itself.<hi type="italic">"Thus, then, men are bowed down, and lords are brought low; and forgive them - no, that Thou wilt not.”</hi> The consecutive futures depict the judgment, as one which would follow by inward necessity from the worldly and ungodly glory of the existing state of things. The future is frequently used in this way (for example, in Isa 9:7.). It was a judgment by which small and great, i.e., the people in all its classes, were brought down from their false eminence. <hi type="italic">“Men”</hi> and <hi type="italic">“lords”</hi> (<hi type="italic">âdâm</hi> and <hi type="italic">ish</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.15">Isa 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.3">Psa 49:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Prov.8.4">Pro 8:4</reference>, and like άνθρωπος and ανήρ in the Attic dialect), i.e., men who were lost in the crowd, and men who rose above it - all of them the judgment would throw down to the ground, and that without mercy (<reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev 6:15</reference>). The prophet expresses the conviction (<hi type="italic">al</hi> as in 2Ki 6:27), that on this occasion God neither could nor would take away the sin by forgiving it. There was nothing left for them, therefore, but to carry out the command of the prophet in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.10">Isa 2:10</reference> : <hi type="italic">“Creep into the rock, and bury thyself in the dust, before the terrible look of Jehovah, and before the glory of His majesty.”</hi> The glorious nation would hide itself most ignominiously, when the only true glory of Jehovah, which had been rejected by it, was manifested in judgment. They would conceal themselves in holes of the rocks, as if before a hostile army (Jdg 6:2; <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.6">1Sa 13:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.11">1Sa 14:11</reference>), and bury themselves with their faces in the sand, as if before the fatal <hi type="italic">simōm</hi> of the desert, that they might not have to bear this intolerable sight. And when Jehovah manifested Himself in this way in the fiery glance of judgment, the result summed up in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa 2:11</reference> must follow: <hi type="italic">“The people’s eyes of haughtiness are humbled, and the pride of their lords is bowed down; and Jehovah, He only, stands exalted in that day.”</hi> The result of the process of judgment is expressed in perfects: <hi type="italic">nisgab</hi> is the third <hi type="italic">pers. praet.</hi>, not the participle: Jehovah “is exalted,” i.e., shows Himself as exalted, whilst the haughty conduct of the people is brought down (<hi type="italic">shâphel</hi> is a verb, not an adjective; it is construed in the singular by attraction, and either refers to <hi type="italic">âdâm</hi>, man or people: Ges. §148, 1; or what is more probable, to the logical unity of the compound notion which is taken as subject, the <hi type="italic">constr.</hi> <hi type="italic">ad synesin s. sensum</hi>: Thiersch, §118), and the pride of the lords is bowed down (<hi type="italic">shach</hi> = <hi type="italic">shâchach</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.9.13">Job 9:13</reference>). The first strophe of the proclamation of judgment appended to the prophetic saying in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Isa 2:2-4</reference> is here brought to a close. The second strophe reaches to <reference osisRef="Isa.2.17">Isa 2:17</reference>, where <reference osisRef="Isa.2.11">Isa 2:11</reference> is repeated as a concluding verse.
entries.75555a670c3f052076e392041548204641d25ba8: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.12">Isa 2:12</reference> <div eID="gen12818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12819" type="x-p"/> The expression <hi type="italic">“that day”</hi> suggests the inquiry, What day is referred to? The prophet answers this question in the second strophe. <hi type="italic">“For Jehovah of hosts hath a day over everything towering and lofty, and over everything exalted; and it becomes low.”</hi> <hi type="italic">“Jehovah hath a day”</hi> (<hi type="italic">yom</hi> <hi type="italic">layehovah</hi>), lit., there is to Jehovah a day, which already exists as a finished divine thought in that wisdom by which the course of history is guided (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>), the secret of which He revealed to the prophets, who from the time of Obadiah and Joel downwards proclaimed that day with one uniform watchword. But when the time appointed for that day should arrive, it would pass out of the secret of eternity into the history of time - a day of world-wide judgment, which would pass, through the omnipotence with which Jehovah rules over the hither as well as lower spheres of the whole creation, upon all worldly glory, and it would be brought low (<hi type="italic">shaphel</hi>). The current accentuation of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.2.12">Isa 2:12</reference></hi> is wrong; correct MSS have על with <hi type="italic">mercha</hi>, כל־נשׂא with <hi type="italic">tifcha</hi>. The word <hi type="italic">v'shâphel</hi> (third pers. praet. with the root-vowel <hi type="italic">ee</hi>) acquires the force of a future, although no grammatical future precedes it, from the future character of the day itself: “and it will sink down” (Ges. §126, 4).
entries.e992759ed819afccbe0816be99c49d9598985f31: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.13-Isa.2.14">Isa 2:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen12819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12820" type="x-p"/> The prophet then proceeds to enumerate all the high things upon which that day would fall, arranging them two and two, and binding them in pairs by a double correlative <hi type="italic">Vav</hi>. The day of Jehovah comes, as the first two pairs affirm, upon everything lofty in nature. <hi type="italic">“As upon all the cedars of Lebanon, the lofty and exalted, so upon all the oaks of Bashan. As upon all mountains, the lofty ones, so upon all hills the exalted ones.”</hi> But wherefore upon all this majestic beauty of nature? Is all this merely figurative? Knobel regards it as merely a figurative description of the grand buildings of the time of Uzziah and Jotham, in the erection of which wood had been used from Lebanon as well as from Bashan, on the western slopes of which the old shady oaks (<hi type="italic">sindiân</hi> and <hi type="italic">ballūt</hi>) are flourishing still.<note placement="foot">On the meaning of the name of this region, <hi type="italic">Bashan</hi> (<hi type="italic">Basanitis</hi>), see <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job</hi>, Appendix, Eng. Tr.</note> <div eID="gen12820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12821" type="x-p"/> But the idea that trees can be used to signify the houses built with the good obtained from them, is one that cannot be sustained from <reference osisRef="Isa.9.9">Isa 9:9</reference> (10.), where the reference is not to houses built of sycamore and cedar wood, but to trunks of trees of the king mentioned; nor even from <reference osisRef="Nah.2.4">Nah 2:4</reference> (3.), where <hi type="italic">habberoshim</hi> refers to the fir lances which are brandished about in haughty thirst for battle. So again mountains and hills cannot denote the castles and fortifications built upon them, more especially as these are expressly mentioned in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.15">Isa 2:15</reference> in the most literal terms. In order to understand the prophet, we must bear in mind what the Scriptures invariably assume, from their first chapter to the very close, namely, that the totality of nature is bound up with man in one common history; that man and the totality of nature are inseparably connected together as centre and circumference; that this circumference is affected by the sin which proceeds from man, as well as by the anger or the mercy which proceeds from God to man; that the judgments of God, as the history of the nations proves, involve in fellow-suffering even that part of the creation which is not free; and that this participation in the “corruption” (<hi type="italic">phthora</hi>) and “glory” (<hi type="italic">doxa</hi>) of humanity will come out with peculiar distinctness and force at the close of the world’s history, in a manner corresponding to the commencement; and lastly, that the world in its present condition needs a <hi type="italic">palingenesia</hi>, or regeneration, quite as much as the corporeal nature of man, before it can become an object of good pleasure on the part of God. We cannot be surprised, therefore, that, in accordance with this fundamental view of the Scriptures, when the judgment of God fell upon Israel, it should also be described as going down to the land of Israel, and as overthrowing not only the false glory of the nation itself, but everything glorious in the surrounding nature, which had been made to minister to its national pride and love of show, and to which its sin adhered in many different ways. What the prophet foretold began to be fulfilled even in the Assyrian wars. The cedar woods of Lebanon were unsparingly destroyed; the heights and valleys of the land were trodden down and laid waste; and, in the period of the great empires which commenced with Tiglath-pileser, the Holy Land was reduced to a shadow of its former promised beauty.
entries.352001c1a68d9b0b866b5ef47cddd781f1fa3f56: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.15-Isa.2.16">Isa 2:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen12821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12822" type="x-p"/> The glory of nature is followed by what is lofty and glorious in the world of men, such as magnificent fortifications, grand commercial buildings, and treasures which minister to the lust of the eye. <hi type="italic">“As upon every high tower, so upon every fortified wall. As upon all ships of Tarshish, so upon all works of curiosity.”</hi> It was by erecting fortifications for offence and defence, both lofty and steep (<hi type="italic">bâzur</hi>, <hi type="italic">praeruptus</hi>, from <hi type="italic">bâzar</hi>, <hi type="italic">abrumpere</hi>, <hi type="italic">secernere</hi>), that Uzziah and Jotham especially endeavoured to serve Jerusalem and the land at large. The chronicler relates, with reference to Uzziah, in 2 Chron 26, that he built strong towers above “the corner-gate, the valley-gate, and the southern point of the cheesemakers’ hollow,” and fortified these places, which had probably been till that time the weakest points in Jerusalem; also that he built towers in the desert (probably in the desert between Beersheba and Gaza, to increase the safety of the land, and the numerous flocks which were pastured in the <hi type="italic">shephelah</hi>, i.e., the western portion of southern Palestine). With regard to Jotham, it is related in both the book of Kings (2Ki 15:32.) and the Chronicles, that he built the upper gate of the temple; and in the Chronicles (<reference osisRef="2Chr.27.1-2Chr.27.9">2Ch 27:1-9</reference>) that he fortified the <hi type="italic">'Ofel</hi>, i.e., the southern spur of the temple hill, still more strongly, and built cities on the mountains of Judah, and erected castles and towers in the forests (to watch for hostile attacks and ward them off). Hezekiah also distinguished himself by building enterprises of this kind (<reference osisRef="2Chr.32.27-2Chr.32.30">2Ch 32:27-30</reference>). But the allusion to the ships of Tarshish takes us to the times of Uzziah and Jotham, and not to those of Hezekiah (as <reference osisRef="Ps.48.7">Psa 48:7</reference> does to the time of Jehoshaphat); for the seaport town of Elath, which was recovered by Uzziah, was lost again to the kingdom of Judah during the reign of Ahaz. Jewish ships sailed from this Elath (Ailath) through the Red Sea and round the coast of Africa to the harbour of Tartessus, the ancient Phoenician emporium of the maritime region watered by the Baetis (Guadalquivir), which abounded in silver, and then returned through the Pillars of Hercules (the Straits of Gibraltar: vid., Duncker, <hi type="italic">Gesch</hi>. i. 312-315). It was to these Tartessus vessels that the expression “ships of Tarshish” primarily referred, though it was afterwards probably applied to mercantile ships in general. The following expression, “works of curiosity” (<hi type="italic">sechiyyoth</hi> <hi type="italic">hachemdah</hi>), is taken in far too restricted a sense by those who limit it, as the lxx have done, to the ships already spoken of, or understand it, as Gesenius does, as referring to beautiful flags. Jerome’s rendering is correct: “<hi type="italic">et super omne quod visu pulcrum est</hi>” (and upon everything beautiful to look at); <hi type="italic">seciyyâh</hi>, from <hi type="italic">sâcâh</hi>, to look, is sight generally. The reference therefore is to all kinds of works of art, whether in sculpture or paintings (<hi type="italic">mascith</hi> is used of both), which delighted the observer by their imposing, tasteful appearance. Possibly, however, there is a more especial reference to curiosities of art and nature, which were brought by the trading vessels from foreign lands. <div eID="gen12822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12823" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.17">Isa 2:17</reference> closes the second strophe of the proclamation of judgment appended to the earlier prophetic word: <hi type="italic">“And the haughtiness of the people is bowed down, and the pride of the lords brought low; and Jehovah, He alone, stands exalted on that day.”</hi> The closing refrain only varies a little from Isa 2:11. The subjects of the verbs are transposed. With a feminine noun denoting a thing, it is almost a rule that the predicate shall be placed before it in masculine (Ges. §147, <hi type="italic">a</hi>).
entries.a385dee9e5f9bbea131b1244504d103da50954c6: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.18">Isa 2:18</reference> <div eID="gen12823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12824" type="x-p"/> The closing refrain of the next two strophes is based upon the concluding clause of Isa 2:10. The proclamation of judgment turns now to the <hi type="italic">elilim</hi>, which, as being at the root of all the evil, occupied the lowest place in the things of which the land was full (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.7">Isa 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.8">Isa 2:8</reference>). In a short v. of one clause consisting of only three words, their future is declared as it were with a lightning-flash. <hi type="italic">“And the idols utterly pass away.”</hi> The translation shows the shortness of the verse, but not the significant <hi type="italic">synallage numeri</hi>. The idols are one and all a mass of nothingness, which will be reduced to absolute annihilation: they will vanish <hi type="italic">Câlil</hi>, i.e., either “they will utterly perish” (<hi type="italic">funditus peribunt</hi>), or, as <hi type="italic">Câlil</hi> is not used adverbially in any other passage, “they will all perish” (<hi type="italic">tota peribunt</hi>, Jdg 20:40) - their images, their worship, even their names and their memory (Zec 13:2).
entries.c8c3bcc48a1a459c9713cd23a9799bca527491e8: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.19">Isa 2:19</reference> <div eID="gen12824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12825" type="x-p"/> What the idolaters themselves will do when Jehovah has so completely deprived their idols of all their divinity, is then described in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.19">Isa 2:19</reference> : <hi type="italic">“And they will creep into caves in the rocks, and cellars in the earth, before the terrible look of Jehovah, and before the glory of His majesty, when He ariseth to put the earth in terror.”</hi> <hi type="italic">Meârâh</hi> is a natural cave, and <hi type="italic">mechillah</hi> a subterraneous excavation: this is apparently the distinction between the two synonyms. <hi type="italic">“To put the earth in terror:”</hi> <hi type="italic">lârotz</hi> <hi type="italic">hâ</hi>-<hi type="italic">aretz</hi>, a significant paronomasia, which can be reproduced in Latin, thus: <hi type="italic">ut terreat terram</hi>. Thus the judgment would fall upon the earth without any limitation, upon men universally (compare the word <hi type="italic">hâ</hi>-<hi type="italic">âdâm</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">Isa 2:20</reference>, which is scarcely ever applied to a single individual (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.15">Jos 14:15</reference>), excepting, of course, the first man, but generally to men, or to the human race) and upon the totality of nature as interwoven in the history of man - one complete whole, in which sin, and therefore wrath, had gained the upper hand. When Jehovah rose up, i.e., stood up from His heavenly throne, to reveal the glory manifested in heaven, and turn its judicial fiery side towards the sinful earth, the earth would receive such a shock as would throw it into a state resembling the chaos of the beginning. We may see very clearly from <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev 6:15</reference>, where this description is borrowed, that the prophet is here describing the last judgment, although from a national point of view and bounded by a national horizon. <div eID="gen12825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12826" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.20">Isa 2:20</reference> forms the commencement to the fourth strophe: <hi type="italic">“In that day will a man cast away his idols of gold and his idols of silver, which they made for him to worship, to the moles and to the bats.”</hi> The traditional text separates <hi type="italic">lachpor</hi> <hi type="italic">peroth</hi> into two words,<note placement="foot">Abulwali=d Parchon and others regard the double word as the singular of a substantive, applied to a particular bird (possibly a woodpecker), as a pecker of fruit (<hi type="italic">peroth</hi>). Kimchi would rather take <hi type="italic">lachpor</hi> as an infinitive (as in <reference osisRef="Josh.2.2">Jos 2:2</reference>), to dig pits; and compares with it the <hi type="italic">talmud</hi>ic word <hi type="italic">pēr</hi>, a pit or grave. No one adopts the rendering “into mouse-holes,” simply because <hi type="italic">pērah</hi>, a mouse (from an Arabic word <hi type="italic">fa'ara</hi>, to dig, or root up), was not a Hebrew word at all, but was adopted at a later period from the Arabic (hence the Hebraeo-Arabic <hi type="italic">purah</hi>, a mousetrap).</note> though without its being possible to discover what they are supposed to mean. The reason for the separation was simply the fact that <hi type="italic">plurilitera</hi> were at one time altogether misunderstood and regarded as <hi type="italic">Composita</hi>: for other <hi type="italic">plurilitera</hi>, written as two words, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa 61:1</reference>; Hos 4:18; Jer 46:20. The prophet certainly pronounced the word <hi type="italic">lachparpâroth</hi> (Ewald, §157,<hi type="italic">c</hi>); and <hi type="italic">Chapharpârâh</hi> is apparently a <hi type="italic">mole</hi> (lit. thrower up of the soil), <hi type="italic">talpa</hi>, as it is rendered by Jerome and interpreted by Rashi. Gesenius and Knobel, however, have raised this objection, that the mole is never found in houses. But are we necessarily to assume that they would throw their idols into lumber-rooms, and not hide them in holes and crevices out of doors? The mole, the shrew-mouse, and the bat, whose name (<hi type="italic">atalleph</hi>) is regarded by Schultens as a compound word (<hi type="italic">atal</hi>-<hi type="italic">eph</hi>, night-bird), are generically related, according to both ancient and modern naturalists. Bats are to birds what moles are to the smaller beasts of prey (vid., Levysohn, <hi type="italic">Zoologie des Talmud</hi>, p. 102). The lxx combine with these two words <hi type="italic">l'hishtachavoth</hi> (to worship). Malbim and Luzzatto adopt this rendering, and understand the words to mean that they would sink down to the most absurd descriptions of animal worship. But the accentuation, which does not divide the v. at עשׂוּ־לו, as we should expect if this were the meaning, is based upon the correct interpretation. The idolaters, convinced of the worthlessness of their idols through the judicial interposition of God, and enraged at the disastrous manner in which they had been deceived, would throw away with curses the images of gold and silver which artists’ hands had made according to their instructions, and hide them in the holes of bats and in mole-hills, to conceal them from the eyes of the Judge, and then take refuge there themselves after ridding themselves of this useless and damnable burden.
entries.e1b7f9480664a096a9e04ae478c8c8ec8dd21e9e: <reference osisRef="Isa.2.21-Isa.2.22">Isa 2:21-22</reference> <hi type="italic">“To creep into the cavities of the stone-blocks, and into the clefts of the rocks, before the terrible look of Jehovah, and before the glory of His majesty, when He arises to put the earth in terror.”</hi> Thus ends the fourth strophe of this “<hi type="italic">dies irae, dies illa</hi>,” which is appended to the earlier prophetic word. But there follows, as an <hi type="italic">epiphonem</hi>, this <hi type="italic">nota bene</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.22">Isa 2:22</reference> : <hi type="italic">Oh, then, let man go, in whose nose is a breath; for what is he estimated at?</hi> The Septuagint leaves this v. out altogether. But was it so utterly unintelligible then? Jerome adopted a false pointing, and has therefore given this marvellous rendering: <hi type="italic">excelsus</hi> (<hi type="italic">bâmâh</hi>!) <hi type="italic">reputatus est ipse</hi>, by which Luther was apparently misled. But if we look backwards and forwards, it is impossible to mistake the meaning of the verse, which must be regarded not only as the resultant of what precedes it, but also as the transition to what follows. It is preceded by the prediction of the utter demolition of everything which ministers to the pride and vain confidence of men; and in Isa 3:1. the same prediction is resumed, with a more special reference to the Jewish state, from which Jehovah is about to take away every prop, so that it shall utterly collapse. Accordingly the prophet exhorts, in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.22">Isa 2:22</reference>, to a renunciation of trust in man, and everything belonging to him, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.8-Ps.118.9">Psa 118:8-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.146.3">Psa 146:3</reference>, and Jer 17:5. The construction is as general as that of a gnome. The dat. <hi type="italic">Commodi</hi> לכם (Ges. §154, 3,<hi type="italic">e</hi>) renders the exhortation both friendly and urgent: from regard to yourselves, for your own good, for your own salvation, desist from man, i.e., from your confidence in him, in whose nose (<hi type="italic">in cujus naso</hi>, the singular, as in <reference osisRef="Job.27.3">Job 27:3</reference>; whereas the plural is used in <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen 2:7</reference> in the same sense, <hi type="italic">in nares ejus</hi>, “into his nostrils”) is a breath, a breath of life, which God gave to him, and can take back as soon as He will (<reference osisRef="Job.34.14">Job 34:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.29">Psa 104:29</reference>). Upon the breath, which passes out and in through his nose, his whole earthly existence is suspended; and this, when once lost, is gone for ever (<reference osisRef="Job.7.7">Job 7:7</reference>). It is upon this breath, therefore, that all the confidence placed in man must rest - a bad soil and foundation! Under these conditions, and with this liability to perish in a moment, the worth of man as a ground of confidence is really nothing. This thought is expressed here in the form of a question: At (for) what is he estimated, or to be estimated? The passive participle <hi type="italic">nechshâb</hi> combines with the idea of the actual (<hi type="italic">aestimatus</hi>) that of the necessary (<hi type="italic">aestimandus</hi>), and also of the possible or suitable (<hi type="italic">aestimabilis</hi>); and that all the more because the Semitic languages have no special forms for the latter notions. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> <hi type="italic">pretı̄</hi>, corresponding to the Latin genitive (<hi type="italic">quanti</hi>) or ablative (<hi type="italic">quanto</hi>) - a modification of the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> <hi type="italic">instrumenti</hi>, the price being regarded as the medium of exchange or purchase: “at what is he estimated,” not with what is he compared, which would be expressed by <hi type="italic">‛eth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">Isa 53:12</reference>; compare μετά, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.37">Luk 22:37</reference>) or <hi type="italic">‛im</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.88.5">Psa 88:5</reference>). The word is בּמּה, not בּמּה, because this looser form is only found in cases where a relative clause follows (<hi type="italic">eo quod</hi>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.22">Ecc 3:22</reference>), and not <hi type="italic">bama=h</hi>, because this termination with <hi type="italic">ā</hi> is used exclusively where the next word begins with <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi>, or where it is a pausal word (as in 1Ki 22:21); in every other case we have <hi type="italic">bammeh</hi>. The question introduced with this <hi type="italic">quanto</hi> (<hi type="italic">quanti</hi>), “at what,” cannot be answered by any positive definition of value. The worth of man, regarded in himself, and altogether apart from God, is really nothing. <div eID="gen12826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12827" type="x-p"/> The proclamation of judgment pauses at this <hi type="italic">porisma</hi>, but only for the purpose of gathering fresh strength. The prophet has foretold in four strophes the judgment of God upon every exalted thing in the <hi type="italic">kosmos</hi> that has fallen away from communion with God, just as Amos commences his book with a round of judgments, which are uttered in seven strophes of uniform scope, bursting like seven thunder-claps upon the nations of the existing stage of history. The seventh stroke falls upon Judah, over which the thunderstorm rests after finding such abundant booty. And in the same manner Isaiah, in the instance before us, reduces the universal proclamation of judgment to one more especially affecting Judah and Jerusalem. The current of the address breaks through the bounds of the strophe; and the exhortation in <reference osisRef="Isa.2.22">Isa 2:22</reference> not to trust in man, the reason for which is assigned in what precedes, also forms a transition from the universal proclamation of judgment to the more special one in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Isa 3:1</reference>, where the prophet assigns a fresh ground for the exhortation.  <chapter eID="Isa.2"/> <div eID="gen12827" type="x-p"/>

entries.9e5f42764a4e74fee116324adbf61aa4d55627fb: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.2.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.2.1" sID="gen40572" type="section"/> <div sID="gen40573" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw</hi> This prophecy is a confirmation of that doctrine which we had a little before, concerning the restoration of the Church. For since it is difficult to cherish the hope of safety, when we are, as it were, in the midst of destruction, while the wrath of God burns and consumes everything far and wide, or while his threatenings strike terror into our minds, at such a period the bare promises are hardly sufficient to support us and to allay our fears. For this reason the Lord determined that to the consolation which had already been proclaimed there should be added this special vision, by way of confirmation, in order to make it more certain and undoubted that, whatever calamities might arise, his Church would never perish. I have no doubt, therefore, but that this vision agrees with what is stated in the 26th and 27th verses of the former chapter.<div eID="gen40573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40574" type="x-p"/>Hence we learn what was the advantage and design of <hi type="italic">visions</hi>; for since doctrine sometimes has not sufficient weight with us, God therefore adds <hi type="italic">visions</hi>, that by means of them he may seal his doctrine to us. Since, therefore, this vision is connected with the former promise, we learn from it this useful doctrine, that all visions of every kind which God formerly gave to his Prophets must be joined to the promises in such a manner as to be seals of them. And thus we perceive more and more the astonishing goodness of God, that, not satisfied with giving us his bare word, he places before our eyes, as it were, representations of the events.<div eID="gen40574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40575" type="x-p"/>He has added a confirmation, that the restoration of the Church is a matter of very great importance, and necessary to be known. For where is the truth of the Lord, where is faith, if there be no Church? If there be none, it follows that God is a liar, and that everything contained in his word is false. But as God frequently shows, by striking proofs, that he preserves the Church by unknown methods and without the assistance of men, so he now declares by a remarkable prediction that he will do this.<div eID="gen40575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40576" type="x-p"/>There were two purposes to be served by this prediction. First, since Isaiah, and others who came after him, were unceasingly to proclaim terror, on account of the obstinate wickedness of the people, until the temple should be burnt, and the city destroyed, and the Jews carried into captivity, it was necessary that such severity should be mitigated towards believers by some consolation of hope. Secondly, as they were to languish in captivity, and as their minds were shaken, even after their return, by a succession of varied calamities, and at length were almost overwhelmed with despair by the dreadful desolation and confusion, they might a hundred times have fainted, if they had not been upheld. As to those who had already fallen, they were raised up and confirmed by the promised restoration, to such an extent, at least, that they retained among them the practice of calling on God, which is the only and undoubted remedy for the worst of evils. <foreign xml:lang="he">הדבר</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">haddabar</hi>,) <hi type="italic">the word</hi>, is rendered by some interpreters <hi type="italic">the thing</hi>, which accords with the general signification of this term; but it is better to view it as denoting a divine purpose. Isaiah says that it was revealed to him by a special vision.<div eID="gen40576" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.2.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen40572" osisID="Isa.2.1" type="section"/>
entries.d454ad29cc365179b2703c391c819fa1efec7362: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.2.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.2.2" sID="gen40577" type="section"/> <div sID="gen40578" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">And it shall come to pass in the last of the days</hi> <note n="35"> <div sID="gen40579" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">In the last days</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen40579" type="x-p"/> </note> When he mentions the end or completion of days, let us remember that he is speaking of the kingdom of Christ; and we ought also to understand why he gives to the kingdom of Christ this appellation. It was because till that time everything might be said to be in a state of suspense, that the people might not fix their eyes on the present condition of things, which was only a shadow, but on the Redeemer, by whom the reality would be declared. Since Christ came, therefore, if that time be compared with ours, we have actually arrived at <hi type="italic">the end of ages</hi>. It was the duty of the fathers who lived at that time to go, as it were, with outstretched arms to Christ; and since the restoration of all things depended on his coming, it is with good reason that they are enjoined to extend their hope to that period.
